about: How they're connected: 2-3 sentences per connection (3+ shared papers, different concept types, no placeholders), written by AI (Claude) from the shared papers' study details in study_details.json. [Label](paper_id) marks a cited paper.

6576|6598.text: Mostly interviews or case-study observation inside companies, with no assigned task; the practitioners' own work is examined. Topics include how information is found, how methods are adopted and how knowledge passes between people. Designers leaned on memory and experience for information ([Court et al., 1995](1570)), experienced designers used analogies differently from novices ([Ahmed & Christensen, 2008](430)), and three company teams relied on benchmarking and reverse engineering ([Lauff et al., 2018](915)).

6576|6600.text: Practitioner ideation studies range from observed sessions to industry case studies. An experienced designer drew about 55 percent of ideas from analogies while a student fixated on one solution [Shah et al., 1993](1522), and in packaging teams, ideas reaching stage-gate concepts dropped after the first 20 minutes [Howard et al., 2008](434). Expertise effects vary: novice and experienced aerial-robot designers did not differ in idea quantity or originality [Tan et al., 2022](825).

6576|6601.text: These three studies are computational or tool-based and differ widely. Practitioners' knowledge was used to bound an optimizer, cutting trial iterations versus human operators and a standard optimizer ([Dong et al., 2025](1449)). Satellite-design experts used an exploration tool, and different learning measures captured different knowledge ([Bang & Selva, 2020](1181)). An automated turbine design process was compared with an industrial case ([Jarrett et al., 2002](218)).

6576|6603.text: Practitioner interviews here cover tools, design methods, empathy and founders' resources rather than a shared design problem. Practitioners found and judged design methods in similar ways, treating efficacy as the key criterion [Gericke et al., 2015](1053), and designers used mixed tools following a capture, reflect and share cycle [Oehlberg et al., 2011](623). Preference accuracy showed no significant link to user satisfaction [Johnson et al., 2023](28).

6576|6604.text: Surveys and questionnaires are used with industry professionals and instructors to learn current practice, mostly with no design problem set. They report which methods practitioners know and find useful ([Yang, 2007](386)), that designers prefer creative ideas but select informally ([Toh et al., 2015](1045)), and that outsourced-design success is judged mainly by relationship quality and client satisfaction ([Palm & Whitney, 2013](794)). Questionnaires also accompany interviews, tool tests, and experiments ([Fillingim et al., 2018](963)).

6576|6611.text: Practitioners such as engineers, designers and executives rated or screened designs, concepts, sounds and shapes on set criteria, in surveys, workshops and case studies. Examples include perceived style similarity of product shapes ([Culbertson & Simpson, 2014](1151)) and concept screening ([Zheng & Miller, 2019](964)). Findings often point to bias or disagreement: individual FMEA scores tracked later failures poorly ([Foster, 2012](737)), and ownership bias appeared only for low-rated ideas ([Zheng & Miller, 2018](971)).

6576|6616.text: Practitioners were interviewed about real projects and work practices, mostly with no design task, across automotive, nuclear, farming and startup settings. Topics included how disciplines perceive products differently ([Cagan et al., 2001](188)), where design principles come from ([Verma, 2017](1057)), and empathy toward users ([Surma-aho et al., 2019](1040)). Interviews were often paired with surveys or observation, and findings are mainly thematic.

6576|6617.text: This overlap is thin: pairwise comparisons build perceptual or variety measures, with practitioners rarely the main sample. Participants rating switch pairs showed four parameters explained most perceived variation in feel [Buttolo et al., 2006](544), and raters' pairwise variety judgments aligned better with a Herfindahl index than tree-based metrics [Ahmed et al., 2019](936). Truck drivers' VR and 2D dashboard ratings differed [Tovares et al., 2013](765).

6576|6618.text: Practitioners are recorded thinking aloud while designing or redesigning, and analysts code the transcripts into activities, information handled or problem maps. Experts attended to a richer set of problem attributes and relations than a novice [Dinar et al., 2011](636), and experts followed a similar strategy but treated evaluation as secondary [Motte et al., 2004](582). Designers who specified more behavior entities scored higher on a divergent-thinking test [Danielescu et al., 2012](682).

6576|6663.text: Practitioners such as mechanical designers and product designers took part in structured analytic or problem-solving work in these studies, with small samples. Designers satisfied given constraints routinely, and quality differences came from constraints they added ([Stauffer & Slaughterbeck-Hyde, 1989](1746)); experts judged a computer-built patent structure sensible ([Fu et al., 2013](785)); and EEG activation was higher when designing than when problem-solving ([Vieira et al., 2019](1055)).

6576|6682.text: Expert mechanical designers read mechanical drawings aloud in observational studies that sometimes compared them with graduate students or novices. Experts reasoned backward from the overall function, and reasoning forward from components was costly and rarely correct, especially for novices ([Waldron et al., 1989](1745); [Chovan & Waldron, 1990](1337)). Five experienced designers' descriptions were also analyzed for the geometric attributes that distinguish features ([Chovan & Waldron, 1991](1360)).

6576|6725.text: These papers share experienced designers working with information or stimuli before generating ideas, with little direct test of a priming activity. Designers grouped information differently but all judged it by relevance to constraints, resources or user requirements ([Damen & Toh, 2019](972)), organized it as clusters, relations or nests linked to idea features ([Toh & Damen, 2020](1197)), and professionals accepted more search results as expected than students did ([Kwon et al., 2022](833)).

6576|6726.text: The overlap is small and varied: practitioners and experts interacted with a product, tool or prototype, and studies looked at gaps, usefulness or acceptance. Gap analysis of tractor operation flagged potential unsafe use, mostly in clutch release and reverser lever use [Murakami et al., 2014](1147), and expert users of a keyword-network discovery tool all found novel items [Chen et al., 2017](910). Automotive designers wanted generative AI tools that fit team workflows [Wang et al., 2024](80).

6576|6729.text: Experienced engineers and designers are interviewed in industry settings about how they decide, find information or run development processes. Many interviews concern information use: aerospace experts kept large personal stores and distrusted company libraries ([Lowe et al., 1999](1596)), and open source designers described new information types tied to coordination ([Yi et al., 2019](1110)). Others looked at methods, with automotive engineers relying on unstructured decisions yet wanting more structure ([Gustavsson & Sterner, 2008](472)).

6576|6869.text: Practitioners appear with building or prototyping, but only loosely. One workshop had users and designers build 3D models of an existing portal to capture their differing perceptions ([Helminen et al., 2010](627)). Engineers at a Rwandan firm were interviewed about prototyping, which they used to make functional models iteratively ([Chou & Austin-Breneman, 2017](1050)). Founders built cardboard chairs for partners, with no significant link between preference accuracy and satisfaction ([Johnson et al., 2023](28)).

6576|7828.text: Interviews, surveys and case studies of company staff dominate, showing how development runs and where it stalls. Collaboration problems recurred across six Silicon Valley firms ([Beskow, 2000](104)), two furniture firms lacked a formal process ([Medeiros et al., 2009](490)), and engineers followed implicit procedures beside written ones ([Jensen & Ahmed, 2009](519)). Automotive firms reported more concurrent engineering than maritime ones ([Smith et al., 2000](119)).

6576|7834.text: Washing machine tasks give practitioners a concrete design setting, though the studies differ in focus. Mechanical engineers designed a washing-machine table drive while heart rate was recorded, and methodical and non-methodical designers did not differ in time or quality ([Rückert & Springer, 1994](1509)). CAD users were slower and sketched more ([Lam et al., 1994](1511)); functional decomposition did not correlate with engineers' grades for a clothes washer ([Booth et al., 2015](977)).

6576|7855.text: These five studies combine practitioners with project-style design work, but few are actual capstone courses. One had mid-career graduate student teams, where falling requirement risk predicted project success ([Bao et al., 2015](1072)). Others observed or interviewed professionals: aerospace engineers' information requests ([Aurisicchio et al., 2006](363)) and microfluidic engineers who began from an existing solution and searched for problems ([Lee et al., 2018](975)).

6576|7876.text: Practitioner studies in the automotive setting are mostly interviews and case studies about decisions, perceptions and preferences rather than vehicle form tests. Engineers, studio designers and marketers described the same products in different terms, creating perceptual gaps [Cagan et al., 2001](188), and multiattribute rankings of material options depended strongly on engineers' subjective preferences [Thurston, 1991](1394). Novices described electric vehicle sounds by character and experts by composition [Petiot et al., 2013](787).

6576|8018.text: Professionals discuss or work on consumer products in interviews, field case studies, and a few experiments. Engineers, designers, and marketers described the same products in different terms, producing goal conflicts ([Cagan et al., 2001](188)). Observed teams in three companies relied mainly on benchmarking and reverse engineering and produced evolutionary products ([Lauff et al., 2018](915)). Another study tested storyboards of an irrigation controller with farmers, who responded positively ([Zande et al., 2022](877)).

6576|8049.text: These studies watched practitioners, mostly mechanical or aerospace designers, working with mechanical parts and drawings, usually by observation or think-aloud rather than CAD modification tasks. Experts reasoned back from overall function more successfully than novices ([Waldron et al., 1989](1745)), sought information missing from blueprints ([Kuffner & Ullman, 1990](1346)), and in [Brennan et al., 2021](860) a workshop shifted process choice but not feature choices.

6576|8219.text: The overlap is small: practitioners working on or evaluating medical device designs in different settings. Experienced workshop groups designing a blood sampling product mostly had information gaps about the knowledge base and design process early on [Waldron & Brooks, 1994](1527), and engineers at an ultrasound company rated style similarity of transducer handles, with strain relief angle dominant [Culbertson & Simpson, 2014](1151).

6576|8224.text: Practitioners and machinery appear together in observation, case-study and computational work on equipment such as dipping machines, turbines and roll-forming lines. Designers sought information missing from blueprints, with 45% of questions and conjectures left unconfirmed ([Kuffner & Ullman, 1990](1346)), and engineers in Rwanda prototyped through simple iteration despite resource limits ([Chou & Austin-Breneman, 2017](1050)). Two computational studies reported efficiency gains over human or industrial baselines ([Jarrett et al., 2002](218); [Dong et al., 2025](1449)).

6576|8230.text: Practitioners' rules of thumb and shortcuts are studied through interviews and protocol analysis. Expert space-mission engineers stated 101 heuristics, and their ratings of frequency of use, reliability and evolution were correlated ([Fillingim et al., 2018](963)). Mechanical designers largely met given constraints routinely, with quality differences tied to constraints they added themselves ([Stauffer & Slaughterbeck-Hyde, 1989](1746)). Groups selecting concepts spent little time weighting criteria ([Girod et al., 2000](92)).

6576|8231.text: Practitioners' judgments are studied through metrics and case reviews rather than direct tests of heuristics. Engineers' individual risk scores in failure analysis correlated poorly with group scores and later failures, which the author reads as availability bias ([Foster, 2012](737)). Team perceptions of manufacturability differed from computed metrics and shaped decisions when metrics were unavailable ([Hight et al., 1995](1563)).

6576|8233.text: Practitioner studies touching metacognition mostly use protocols, interviews and EEG to see how experts reason about their own process. Expert aerospace designers used strategic questions to set up and refine their reasoning questions [Aurisicchio et al., 2007](395), and the ability to state design principles grew with the number of prior designs [Verma, 2017](1057). In professional designers, metacognitive speech coincided with higher alpha and beta power than spontaneous or deliberate speech [Vieira et al., 2023](78).

6576|8234.text: Studies of practitioners touched on memory mainly as reliance on what designers already know, observed in case studies, interviews and think-aloud work, not controlled retrieval tests. Designers drew heavily on their own memory and experience when seeking information ([Court et al., 1995](1570)), and experts kept large personal stores while distrusting company libraries ([Lowe et al., 1999](1596)).

6576|8236.text: Practitioner studies of shared understanding are mostly interviews, observation and case studies in companies. Engineers, designers and marketers described the same products differently, creating perceptual gaps [Cagan et al., 2001](188), while communication was hindered by differing disciplinary backgrounds and handovers [Borgman et al., 2023](7). Objects helped cross-functional work by translating information and prompting joint negotiation [Brubaker et al., 2022](815), and designer teams showed four types of sharedness in conversation [Yi et al., 2020](1189).

6576|8237.text: These studies mostly observe teams of professionals or experts and code their conversation or recorded activity. Social exchange made up about 45 percent of utterances in two multidisciplinary teams ([Milne & Leifer, 2000](116)), and novice-expert consultations split roles, with novices driving explanation and experts supplying organizational information ([Deken et al., 2009](521)). In MBA teams, how strongly a person generally triggered ideas in others predicted creative interaction better than past pairwise ratings ([Sosa & Marle, 2010](653)).

6576|8238.text: Practitioner studies of fixation are mostly interviews, surveys, case studies and observation of real projects, with few controlled experiments. Experts in a survey were split on whether analogies cause fixation ([Krager et al., 2011](701)), and experienced designers mostly sought familiar or similar examples ([Miller & Bailey, 2014](1150)). One workshop changed professionals' manufacturing process choice, but not their feature-level choices ([Brennan et al., 2021](860)).

6576|8239.text: Only one study directly paired practitioners with a divergent thinking test: eight expert designers who also thought aloud while designing, where more behavior-focused problem maps went with higher fluency, quality and creativity scores ([Danielescu et al., 2012](682)). Other papers touch divergence more loosely, such as interviews showing academic engineers diverged in problems more than solutions ([Lee et al., 2018](975)) and a NASA team comparing human and AI-assisted ideas ([Koolman et al., 2025](1423)).

6576|8240.text: Practitioners are interviewed or given tasks to show what their experience supplies, from how they describe function to how projects start. Aerospace designers' descriptions mostly matched function taxonomies, yet they discussed issues and process far more than function ([Ahmed & Wallace, 2003](304)); microfluidic engineers began with an existing solution and searched for problems ([Lee et al., 2018](975)); and sound experts described vehicle sounds by composition, novices by character ([Petiot et al., 2013](787)).

6576|8241.text: Practitioner studies here use interviews and surveys on creative drive, risk-taking and team conditions, with motivation measured directly in only some. Among industry professionals, self-rated motivation predicted novelty only with the WordTree method ([Moreno et al., 2015](957)). Willingness to take risks on creative ideas related to education and experience ([Zheng & Miller, 2017](1018)), and a person's general tendency to trigger ideas predicted creative interaction ([Sosa & Marle, 2010](653)).

6576|8246.text: Cognitive style shows up in practitioner studies mostly as personality or creativity measures, or as differences by expertise and culture. Workshop faculty shifted on Myers-Briggs scores toward intuitive, feeling and perceptive preferences ([Wilde, 1993](1550)), and creativity modes could be linked to designers' activity patterns ([Kim et al., 2006](359)). Design processes differed among German, Indian and Chinese designers in ways linked to culture ([Gautam & Blessing, 2009](520)).

6576|8247.text: Practitioner studies of evaluative judgment have people rate, screen or compare designs, with different findings about what experts value. Engineers valued a clarity modifier more than desk workers did when judging photocopies [Shimomura et al., 1996](1743), and practicing engineers' inventiveness rankings matched the SIT conditions in 19 of 20 problems [Horowitz & Maimon, 1997](1670). Executives favored high-feasibility ideas while idea generators did not [Zheng & Miller, 2019](964).

6576|8248.text: Studies of problem framing with experienced designers rely on observation and think-aloud protocols. Problem maps showed the problem and solution spaces evolving, with richer attended attributes for the expert than the novice ([Dinar et al., 2011](636)). Among expert designers, specifying more behavior entities went with higher creativity scores ([Danielescu et al., 2012](682)). Professionals also organized information into clusters, relations, and nests ([Toh & Damen, 2020](1197)).

6576|8249.text: Experienced designers were studied for how they adapt to or search for unexpected information, using interviews, think-aloud and EEG. Practitioners deliberately changed how they handled information across situations ([Damen & Toh, 2021](884)). Professionals found more results as expected and accepted more when searching for inspiration, while students met more unexpected results ([Kwon et al., 2022](833)); metacognitive speech showed higher EEG band power ([Vieira et al., 2023](78)).

6576|8252.text: Empathy is studied in practitioners mainly through interviews, plus a few measurement experiments. Designers described cognitive empathy as improving the accuracy of their user understanding, and affective empathy as raising motivation to help ([Surma-aho et al., 2019](1040)). A quick empathic accuracy measure matched the full version ([Li et al., 2021](856)), while preference accuracy showed no significant link to user satisfaction ([Johnson et al., 2023](28)).

6576|8254.text: Experienced practitioners appear mostly in think-aloud, interview, and observational studies of how reasoning runs during design. Expert designers reasoned inversely from overall function to parts more often and more successfully than novices ([Waldron et al., 1989](1745)). Experts also worked early in concrete parts and treated checking as secondary ([Motte et al., 2004](582)). Aerospace engineers' information requests often needed reasoning, not simple lookup ([Aurisicchio et al., 2006](363)).

6576|8255.text: Practitioner studies touching mental models mostly use think-aloud, interviews and workshops to see how professionals' and novices' understanding differs. Experienced aerospace designers used analogies to reason about function and behavior, while novices mostly transferred information directly ([Ahmed & Christensen, 2008](430)). Engineers, designers and marketers described the same products in different terms ([Cagan et al., 2001](188)), and expert engineers' knowledge networks grew larger with more company experience ([Pollack et al., 2025](1417)).

6576|8256.text: Practitioners were studied through interviews, surveys and observation in settings such as aerospace, automotive, design consulting and AI-supported teams. Trust appeared as an outcome or influence rather than a manipulated variable. Facilitator behaviors correlated positively with team trust and psychological safety ([Witherell et al., 2024](83)); experts in [Lowe et al., 1999](1596) distrusted company libraries, and NASA team members' AI use varied by strategy ([Ma et al., 2024](70)).

6576|8257.text: The clearest links come from observational and think-aloud studies of experienced designers using analogies. In one, the experienced designer drew about 55 percent of ideas from analogies while a student fixated ([Shah et al., 1993](1522)). Experienced aerospace engineers used analogies to solve problems and reason about function, whereas novices mostly transferred information directly ([Ahmed & Christensen, 2008](430)). Other studies touch analogy more loosely, such as expert views on analogy and fixation ([Krager et al., 2011](701)).

6576|8259.text: Practitioners appear with cognitive load mainly in physiological or self-report measures of strain, plus a few interview studies. Mechanical engineers designing a washing-machine drive had heart rate recorded, with evaluating variants and calculating causing the most strain ([Rückert & Springer, 1994](1509)), and CAD users were slower than conventional designers in the companion study ([Lam et al., 1994](1511)). Chemists rated task burden with NASA TLX, and it depended strongly on reagent properties ([Jung & Bruns, 2024](29)).

6576|8261.text: Executive function is not measured directly in these papers, which instead compare how experts plan and regulate their work. Experts followed a similar strategy and treated evaluation and checking as secondary ([Motte et al., 2004](582)), and expert designers spread their activities more effectively than students ([Kim et al., 2006](359)). A conflict-task creativity intervention that worked in person did not replicate online ([Sahar & Shu, 2021](816)).

6576|8267.text: Studies look at how experienced designers learn or capture knowledge while working, through protocols, interviews and tests. One protocol of a ship designer supported a model linking design and learning activities, though the authors call the evidence limited ([Sim & Duffy, 2002](231)); designers used varied tools following a capture, reflect and share cycle ([Oehlberg et al., 2011](623)); and different learning measures captured different knowledge gained by satellite design experts ([Bang & Selva, 2020](1181)).

6576|8269.text: Self-regulation shows up only indirectly in these practitioner studies, through self-ratings of motivation, risk and control. Among industry professionals, self-rated motivation and problem easiness predicted novelty only under one method, and time pressure predicted fluency without a method ([Moreno et al., 2015](957)). Designers saw little control over manufacturing but more over practice and business areas ([Damen et al., 2022](817)); falling requirement risk predicted success ([Bao et al., 2015](1072)).

6576|8274.text: Practitioners' risk attitudes were studied through surveys, selection tasks and interviews, mostly at single companies. Education and experience related to willingness to take creative risks, and R&D staff and managers were more financially risk averse ([Zheng & Miller, 2017](1018)). Professionals avoided risk when screening concepts ([Zheng & Miller, 2019](964)), and interviews linked prototyping reluctance to early-stage barriers ([Mitomi et al., 2023](47)).

6576|8276.text: Psychological safety is studied among professionals in startups, factories and facilitated workshops, using surveys, interviews and observation, so the settings vary widely. Deep-tech founders who perceived their team as more psychologically safe were better at identifying useful resources against obstacles ([Letting et al., 2023](36)), and facilitator behaviors correlated positively with trust and safety in a workshop ([Witherell et al., 2024](83)). A study of Nigerian factories dealt with coordination under scarcity ([Kusimo & Sheppard, 2019](1020)).

6576|8277.text: Experienced designers and engineers are studied through think-aloud protocols, transcript coding or brain recording while working on real or set problems. Strategic questions shaped reasoning questions in aerospace designers ([Aurisicchio et al., 2007](395)), software designers co-evolved problem and solution and mostly searched depth-first ([Ahmed-Kristensen & Babar, 2012](719)), and EEG activation was higher in designing than in problem-solving ([Vieira et al., 2019](1055)). [Takeda et al., 1990](1342) used protocols to track shifts in attention.

6576|8279.text: Practitioners, such as engineers, consultants and drivers, state or rate preferences that researchers turn into utility models or consistency checks. In one case study, a consistency check exposed inconsistent stated preferences in an engineer's drill choices ([Kulok & Lewis, 2005](152)), and material rankings depended strongly on engineers' subjective preferences ([Thurston, 1991](1394)). Truck drivers' ratings in VR differed from those on 2D images across the design space ([Tovares et al., 2013](765)).

6576|8280.text: Experienced practitioners are compared with novices on how prior knowledge shapes what they notice and how they organize information. Experts read mechanical drawings by reasoning backward from overall function, while novices focused on geometry ([Waldron et al., 1989](1745); [Chovan & Waldron, 1990](1337)). Experts attended to a richer set of attributes and relations when formulating a problem ([Dinar et al., 2011](636)).

6576|8281.text: Practitioner studies touching self-efficacy are mostly surveys, interviews and training programs. Educators gained confidence in embedding design justice over a summit [Roeder et al., 2024](66), and trained elementary teachers showed more engineering teaching skills, which the authors link to confidence [Crawford et al., 1995](1569). In industry, self-rated factors rarely predicted ideation outcomes [Moreno et al., 2015](957), and experience related to willingness to take creative risks [Zheng & Miller, 2017](1018).

6576|8294.text: The three papers use experts or mixed samples to link physical features to emotional or aesthetic responses. Four parameters explained most perceived variation in rotary switch feel [Buttolo et al., 2006](544), a fuzzy model of geometric features predicted human aggressiveness ratings of shapes fairly well, with correlation about 0.88 [Achiche & Ahmed, 2008](456), and novices and experts described electric vehicle sounds differently, with wide individual variation [Petiot et al., 2013](787).

6576|8297.text: Information processing is examined through coding of how designers handle information. Six designers handled information at a similar rate, about 8 units per minute ([Baya & Leifer, 1995](1571)). In team conceptual design, social interaction made up about 45 percent of utterances ([Milne & Leifer, 2000](116)). Interviews with open source designers identified information types and coordination archetypes ([Yi et al., 2019](1110)).

6576|8309.text: Few of these studies appear to measure working memory directly; they follow how practitioners handle information while designing, through think-aloud, EEG and interviews. Designers handled information at about 8 dims per minute, with most conceptual time at non-quantitative abstraction ([Baya & Leifer, 1995](1571)); they routinely met given constraints, so quality differed by constraints they added ([Stauffer & Slaughterbeck-Hyde, 1989](1746)); and EEG activation was higher in designing than problem-solving ([Vieira et al., 2019](1055)).

6576|8310.text: Experienced practitioners are studied as holders and sharers of knowledge, via consultations, card sorting and interviews. Experts mainly supplied organizational information and past-design discussion to trainee teams ([Deken et al., 2009](521)). Professional designers judged grouping as better for learning and linking as better for knowledge transfer ([Wang et al., 2021](894)), and operators' trial-and-error knowledge, extracted to guide an optimizer, cut setup iterations ([Dong et al., 2025](1449)).

6576|8366.text: Practitioners' division of work across people, groups or AI tools appears in observation and interview studies of collaborative design and process management. Experienced workshop participants showed many more information gaps than helps or decisions within groups early on ([Waldron & Brooks, 1994](1527)), and a NASA team used generative AI in three ways, from co-design to minimal use ([Ma et al., 2024](70)). Toyota developed designs by narrowing sets of alternatives ([Ward et al., 1994](1589)).

6576|8367.text: Studies of practitioners and expertise mostly compare experts with novices through think-aloud protocols and interviews. Experts reasoned backward from overall function when reading drawings while novices focused on geometry [Chovan & Waldron, 1990](1337), and experienced aerospace engineers used analogies to solve or identify problems while novices mostly transferred information directly [Ahmed & Christensen, 2008](430). Company experience also went with larger knowledge networks [Pollack et al., 2025](1417).

6576|8521.text: Practitioner studies touch ambiguity tolerance only indirectly, through uncertainty and risk attitudes among industry staff. Decisions in a carmaker escalated as uncertainty grew, and limited knowledge of simulation limits led to postponements ([Sissoko et al., 2018](979)). Education and experience related to professionals' willingness to take creative risks ([Zheng & Miller, 2017](1018)), and the main front-end challenge was selling concepts internally ([Elverum et al., 2014](1152)).

6576|8522.text: Practitioner studies touch implicit cognition only indirectly, and they vary widely. Designers reinterpreted vague problems repeatedly through analogy-based shifts [Dzbor & Zdrahal, 2002](253), and prototyping skill depended on individuals and tacit knowledge [Mitomi et al., 2023](47). Better teams converged in language style as meetings progressed [Cannon & Edelman, 2019](1067), and metacognitive speech showed higher alpha and beta power in EEG [Vieira et al., 2023](78).

6576|8523.text: Practitioners are studied mostly through think-aloud protocols and interviews, with attention treated as what they focus on or how it shifts. [Takeda et al., 1990](1342) tracked shifts in engineers' attention with a concept network built from protocols, and [Chovan & Waldron, 1991](1360) found a small set of geometric attributes sufficient to describe drawings. Designers from three countries showed culture-linked process differences ([Gautam & Blessing, 2009](520)).

6576|8524.text: The clearest case is an experiment where design professionals rated teammates' and their own milk-frother ideas, showing ownership bias only for ideas teammates judged low in goodness ([Zheng & Miller, 2018](971)). Other shared studies are interviews or case studies of practice, such as engineers using unstructured methods for decisions ([Gustavsson & Sterner, 2008](472)) and following implicit procedures ([Jensen & Ahmed, 2009](519)). They rarely test bias directly.

6576|8525.text: Practitioners make decisions or seek information when facts are incomplete, observed in design tasks and company meetings. Engineers sought information missing from blueprints, and 45% of 372 questions and conjectures went unconfirmed ([Kuffner & Ullman, 1990](1346)); carmaker decisions were escalated as complexity and uncertainty grew, and limited simulation knowledge postponed some ([Sissoko et al., 2018](979)). A graph grammar search using comparison judgments was tested with simulated and author judgments ([Campbell et al., 2009](510)).

6576|8528.text: Experts think aloud, build out their knowledge, or discuss requirements, and researchers look at how that knowledge is structured. Protocols were turned into a semantic network showing what knowledge designers used and how attention shifted ([Takeda et al., 1990](1342)), experts' sticky-note networks grew fastest while recognizing the problem and ended larger with more company experience ([Pollack et al., 2025](1417)), and experts disagreed on whether some requirements were demands or wishes ([Venkatesh et al., 2025](1429)).

6577|6598.text: Students appear in studies of naturalistic project work, with records or recordings analyzed. Archives from past years drew little access from student teams ([Liang et al., 1998](1648)). In one sponsored project, over half the noun phrases appeared in informal audio and video and only 5 percent in formal reports ([Yen et al., 1999](1623)). Interviews with female makerspace users described learning both design and life skills ([Tomko et al., 2018](1051)).

6577|6600.text: Student participants in mostly controlled experiments generated concepts for set problems such as peanut shellers or milk frothers, while researchers varied a stimulus, method or condition. Studies tested analogies, example solutions, sketching versus building, and individual versus team work, e.g. [Shah et al., 2006](358) and [Viswanathan & Linsey, 2011](608). Results vary: some aids raised novelty, others quality or quantity, and individuals sometimes outperformed teams ([Gyory et al., 2018](1011)).

6577|6601.text: Students work on parameter tuning, truss, drone and similar tasks, usually in controlled experiments that log how they search or compare them with algorithms. Strong performers searched like a tuned annealing algorithm, the weakest near randomly ([Yu et al., 2015](1037)). Integrated optimization tools gave cheaper trusses faster ([Burnell et al., 2017](1022)), and robust optimization widened exploration ([Pillai et al., 2020](1180)). Interacting teams did worse in one study ([McComb et al., 2017](986)).

6577|6603.text: Students appear both as interviewers gathering user needs and as design-team members whose interviews or tool use are studied. Interviews by student teams showed users rarely ranked sustainability first ([Oehlberg et al., 2009](508)), and students wearing a mock prosthesis identified most lead-user and typical-user needs plus extra latent needs ([Vaughan et al., 2014](1163)). One study scored interview quality in practice and field interviews ([Grover et al., 2023](22)).

6577|6604.text: Mostly course-based experiments and design classes where students answer questionnaires alongside a design task, covering risk attitudes, psychological safety or a method's usefulness. Results differ: more risk-averse students generated and chose less creative ideas ([Toh & Miller, 2014](1142)), psychological safety predicted idea quality but not count ([Cole et al., 2020](1190)), and a preference questionnaire used to form teams went with more prize-winning teams ([Wilde, 1997](1694)).

6577|6605.text: Engineering students group system elements into subsystems on paper, usually from a function graph, component graph or function structure. Elements were more likely to be grouped when directly connected or close on the page ([Patel et al., 2022](839)), and representation effects varied across products ([Murphy et al., 2022](895)). Cluster size did not relate to self-efficacy or need for closure ([Patel et al., 2023](59)).

6577|6607.text: Students listed alternate uses for common objects, often as a divergent thinking measure alongside engineering tasks. Fluency and flexibility correlated strongly between a uses test and an engineering ideation test ([Johnson et al., 2015](953)), and freshmen and upperclassmen did not differ in originality ([Bennetts et al., 2017](930)). A scaled uses task lowered fluency but raised correctly scaled blade reuse ideas ([Arabian & Shu, 2021](832)).

6577|6611.text: Students rate, rank, or choose among designs or concepts, often in controlled experiments. Several test the instrument itself: rating scales for design quality were reliable over time in some cases and not in others ([Hyde & Stauffer, 1990](1393)), and absolute ratings beat relative comparison ([Diteman & Stauffer, 1993](1505)). Others show student selections are shaped by risk attitude ([Toh & Miller, 2014](1142)) and ownership bias ([Toh et al., 2015](925)).

6577|6612.text: Students dissected or tore down everyday products such as hair dryers and milk frothers, either to model them or to generate ideas. Dissection gave more novel but lower-quality ideas than visual inspection ([Toh & Miller, 2013](771)), and part reuse tracked idea creativity ([Starkey et al., 2018](943)). Agreement in interaction modeling depended on how clearly interactions were defined ([Tilstra et al., 2010](707)).

6577|6615.text: Graduate and senior students build function structures for household or electromechanical products, sometimes with a rule set or seed model, and the studies score the models or watch how they are built. Models drawn with a grammar scored higher than unaided ones ([Sridharan & Campbell, 2004](337)), and nucleation seeds led to more added functions and flows ([Patel et al., 2017](1034)). Students paused about 38 percent of modeling time ([Patel et al., 2018](1043)).

6577|6616.text: Student studies use interviews mostly as a follow-up to a design or sketching session, to hear why they acted as they did. Interviews supported think-aloud work on biological analogy ([Vakili et al., 2007](375); [Arlitt et al., 2015](941)), product dissection and fixation ([Starkey et al., 2018](943)), and a cultural requirements method that increased stated consideration of user culture ([Agyemang & Turner, 2020](1176)). Findings concern the tested intervention rather than interviewing itself.

6577|6617.text: Students make repeated choices or judgments among design options, and the choices feed a preference model. An interactive genetic algorithm converged on target glass shapes within a tolerable number of generations ([Poirson et al., 2011](706)), a Bayesian optimizer built on pairwise mug-comfort choices matched individuals best when aggregate data was combined with their own ([Nandy & Goucher-Lambert, 2023](53)), and a copula model matched participants' cabin rankings better than an additive model ([Zhou & Jiao, 2013](789)).

6577|6618.text: Student participants think aloud while working on open design problems, and the recordings are coded to describe their process. Studies range from small protocol analyses of information handling ([Baya & Leifer, 1994](1506)) to team-size comparisons, where groups of three scored best on final designs ([Jacobs et al., 2019](1052)). Some link process to outcome: requesting more aspects of information went with better requirement fulfillment ([Wiegers et al., 1996](1730)).

6577|6619.text: Students write reflections in design courses, either as coursework that researchers later code or as a short step inside an experiment. The text has been analyzed for what teams learned ([Radcliffe, 1996](1731)), how they justified decisions ([Loweth et al., 2020](1178)), and mood across a project ([Harris & Toh, 2023](23)). Where reflection was manipulated, writing about intended users became deeper when students drew people in sketches ([Makhlouf et al., 2023](43)).

6577|6628.text: Engineering students take cognitive or spatial tests, or estimation questions, alongside design tasks. Constructive perception and visual reasoning each related to creative design performance, though they were not correlated with each other ([Kim et al., 2005](154)). Spatial visualization scores rose over a semester, mostly after sketching rather than CAD ([Hilton et al., 2018](1101)), while MIT students' estimates spread over 6 to 9 orders of magnitude ([Linder & Flowers, 1996](1733)).

6577|6652.text: Student divergent-thinking tests range from instrument development to experiments that add a manipulation before the test. An eight-question test gave a four-factor structure in factor analysis, though only intrinsic validation was done [Shah et al., 2010](661). An episodic memory induction made alternate-use answers more flexible and elaborate, and repurposing ideas more appropriate and feasible, with no fluency difference [Arabian et al., 2020](1174). GPT-4 gave more ideas but less original individual responses [Medina & Murakami, 2025](1418).

6577|6663.text: Engineering students apply a specified procedure to cases, and outputs are checked against criteria. BOB-UP users pinpointed the affected zone more often than cause-effect chain users, though locating the cause stayed weak ([Russo & Birolini, 2011](606)). Students were about 86 percent accurate with the Four-Box method ([Helms & Goel, 2014](1120)), and guideline order changed the resulting unit cells ([Fazelpour et al., 2017](1014)).

6577|6670.text: Students, alone or mixed with other groups, judge which of several items is most similar, mostly to test how similarity works or how well computed measures match people. Cosine similarity matched human judgments for very similar products at the detailed level, while network measures fit better at the purpose level ([Nandy & Goucher-Lambert, 2021](844)). Human and deep-learning similarity of 3D parts agreed at a coarse level ([Kwon & Goucher-Lambert, 2023](35)).

6577|6672.text: Only one of the three shared papers has study details. Undergraduates developed solutions from an initial idea given as a sketch or as text, and graphical starting ideas yielded more novel, higher-quality ideas ([McKoy et al., 2001](205)). The other two concern sketch-based tools: a Wizard-of-Oz study with professional designers ([Baudoux & Gronier, 2025](1430)) and a sketch recognition paper without details.

6577|6678.text: Students sketch in design courses and experiments, and the sketches are then analyzed or tied to outcomes. More sketches did not mean better outcomes: quantity alone did not predict results in one course ([Elsen et al., 2012](739)), though another linked more sketches to better outcomes ([Das & Yang, 2021](810)). Sketching before listing requirements improved their typology and novelty ([Spivey et al., 2020](1169)), and sketch quality and idea quantity were largely independent ([Weaver et al., 2022](841)).

6577|6682.text: Students appear alongside experts in drawing-reading studies in which participants verbalize what a mechanism diagram shows. Students and novices focused on geometry, whereas experts reasoned back from overall function ([Waldron et al., 1989](1745); [Chovan & Waldron, 1990](1337)). In a blurred-diagram study with senior students, labels sped recognition and attention clustered at object interfaces ([Fuge & Kara, 2009](497)).

6577|6725.text: Students do a short priming step, such as a collage, questionnaire, warm-up drawing or teamwork activity, before ideating, and researchers score the ideas that follow. Collage and questionnaire primes raised the number and effectiveness of sustainability-signaling toaster features ([She & MacDonald, 2012](690)), but collage priming helped only the environmental dimension of washing-machine ideas ([Liao & MacDonald, 2018](1111)). Warm-up sketching eased stress yet left idea counts unchanged ([Hu et al., 2015](945)).

6577|6726.text: Engineering students interacted with software, simulated devices and search platforms in these studies, with different outcomes in each. Multimedia motor software raised test scores ([Reamon & Sheppard, 1999](1626)). Students trusted a simulated smart lock more when the agent's voice matched a gender stereotype for the setting ([Damen & Toh, 2017](1081)), though reaction-time measures showed no such difference ([Damen & Toh, 2018](1039)). Search modality changed search frequency and coverage ([Kwon et al., 2021](842)).

6577|6764.text: Student studies of CAD modification tasks are small experiments and observations of how students edit or redesign parts in CAD. Models carrying 3D design-intent annotations led 104 freshmen to better choices in alteration tasks than unannotated models [Camba et al., 2014](1129), and an inspectability worksheet changed how students removed material in a small additive-manufacturing redesign [Mahan et al., 2020](1204). Paired designers showed more facial emotion than solo designers [Zhou et al., 2019](1079).

6577|6776.text: Students build function structures or similar models, often from disassembled products, and studies check repeatability, mistakes and model size. Half of sub-functions appeared in over 70 percent of students' models [Kurfman et al., 2000](107), and component templates gave fewer mistakes and more functions [Abbott & Lough, 2008](444). Top-down and energy-flow methods beat enumeration for students, but functional decomposition did not track professionals' grades [Booth et al., 2015](977).

6577|6789.text: Students write or elicit requirements in short controlled experiments comparing methods, team sizes and tools. No derivation method was dominant among novices, though methods differed on most metrics ([Renz & Olewnik, 2015](1056)); a taxonomy gave more and better manufacturability requirements for those who followed it ([Gershenson & Stauffer, 1996](1705)); and teams of three and six used more numeric targets than individuals ([Nonso-Anyakwo & Summers, 2025](1439)).

6577|6820.text: Engineering students complete CAD and spatial tasks, alone or in pairs, with model quality or spatial skill as outcomes. Pairs sharing one CAD control made higher-quality, more complete models than pairs working in parallel ([Olechowski et al., 2020](1191)), and larger teams took less calendar time but more person-hours ([Cheng & Olechowski, 2021](854)). Spatial scores rose over a semester, mostly after sketching rather than CAD ([Hilton et al., 2018](1101)).

6577|6838.text: Student participants use blindfolds, earplugs, mitts, or mock limbs, then generate concepts or interview about user needs. After impaired use of alarm clocks, seniors produced more original concepts with no loss of technical quality ([Genco et al., 2011](610)). Guided empathy-tool use found more latent needs than unguided use ([Raviselvam et al., 2018](959)), and simulated extreme-user perspectives surfaced latent needs on all six medical devices ([Raviselvam et al., 2019](952)).

6577|6856.text: Students received instruction in a technique and then did a design or modeling task, in course and lab settings. TRIZ lectures improved the novelty and variety of concepts at both a senior and a graduate sample ([Hernandez et al., 2012](676)), and functional modeling instruction improved graduate mental model scores, with a likely ceiling effect for one product ([Murphy et al., 2019](1004)). An inclusive design scheme helped only to a limited extent ([Sangelkar & McAdams, 2013](772)).

6577|6869.text: Students build towers, Lego devices and launchers from kits, mostly in controlled experiments varying prototyping strategy or prior sketching. Building more prototypes early gave larger gains between first and final tower, with more time pressure ([Neeley et al., 2013](782)), and a prototyping-strategy method helped teams hit a target ([Camburn et al., 2013](792)). Sketching first did not change ball height ([Faas et al., 2014](1133)), nor did extra system-level activity change outcomes ([Ruder & Sobek, 2005](128)).

6577|7834.text: Washing machines serve as a sustainability redesign or evaluation object in these studies. A collage prime produced more environmentally friendly ideas but not social or economic ones ([Liao & MacDonald, 2018](1111)), a chatbot design assistant was mostly rated useful and trustworthy with male and younger participants more skeptical ([Renji et al., 2024](63)), and showing environmental impact moved consumers' valuation from form toward function ([Goucher-Lambert & Cagan, 2014](1122)).

6577|7836.text: Student teams and individuals design truss bridges or similar trusses in software, with researchers tracking quality and how designs change. High-performing teams chose simpler designs and explored small regions thoroughly ([McComb et al., 2014](1148)), and team performance rested mainly on the strongest member ([Brownell et al., 2020](1186)). Integrated optimization tools gave better designs faster ([Burnell et al., 2017](1022)), and confidence in AI suggestions moved with its accuracy ([Chong et al., 2022](845)).

6577|7837.text: The clothes ironing device is a design problem used in function-modeling and morphological-chart studies with engineering students. Students focused on the first columns of a chart regardless of function order ([Chawla & Summers, 2018](955)). Participants paused for about 38% of function modeling time and added elements after most pauses ([Patel et al., 2018](1043)), and a towel-ironing study found function, flow and form similarity all used in analogies ([Arlitt et al., 2015](941)).

6577|7846.text: Students worked on briefs for people with disabilities or older adults, such as book-reaching devices for wheelchair users and window openers, mostly in controlled experiments or course studies. Sketching before listing requirements improved their novelty and typology ([Spivey et al., 2020](1169)), and scrum-story requirements raised solution novelty ([Patel et al., 2021](864)). Others tracked prefrontal brain activity ([Milovanovic et al., 2020](1198)).

6577|7848.text: The paperclip alternate-uses task is used as a quick ideation task for students, mostly to test small manipulations. Classifying or combining earlier ideas raised novelty, classifying more so and with more unique ideas [Kirjavainen & Hölttä-Otto, 2019](924), and an episodic memory induction made uses more flexible and elaborate [Arabian et al., 2020](1174). In a paperclip design problem, building and testing physical models raised the fraction of functional ideas without producing fixation [Viswanathan & Linsey, 2010](649).

6577|7851.text: Student studies on the household recycling sorter mostly use it as a shared brief for function-structure modeling and idea-generation tasks. Students paused about 38 percent of modeling time, adding elements after short pauses and deleting after long ones [Patel et al., 2018](1043); teams of three scored best on final designs while teams of five backtracked most [Jacobs et al., 2019](1052). Students focused on the first chart columns regardless of function order [Chawla & Summers, 2018](955).

6577|7852.text: Engineering students sketch milk-frother ideas in controlled experiments on dissection, risk attitudes, tools and concept selection. Dissecting the frother gave more novel but lower-quality ideas than inspecting it [Toh & Miller, 2013](771), and more risk-averse students generated and chose less creative ideas [Toh & Miller, 2014](1142). Male students selected more of their own ideas than female students [Toh et al., 2015](925), and paper sketches scored higher in quality than tablet sketches [Das et al., 2023](13).

6577|7855.text: Capstone and sponsored course projects are the setting for observational and quasi-experimental studies using design journals, web logs, team messages and grades. System-level idea generation and refinement best predicted quality ([Wilkening & Sobek, 2004](325)), prior-year project archives were rarely reused ([Liang & Leifer, 2000](120)), and a context-indicator method raised combined quality, novelty and feasibility when teams followed it ([Camburn et al., 2012](685)). Wilde's team model explained about 10% of outcome variance ([Freiheit, 2014](1149)).

6577|7856.text: The toaster appears in three student studies with different aims. Students built functional models of a toaster that were highly repeatable, though errors exposed weaknesses in the vocabulary ([Kurfman et al., 2000](107)). In redesign tasks, a collage or questionnaire prime increased sustainability-signaling features ([She & MacDonald, 2012](690)), and a structured quiz increased sustainable design decisions ([Ross et al., 2019](1102)).

6577|7860.text: The food insecurity brief appears in first-year course projects, where students' team conditions were tracked alongside concept generation. Psychological safety stabilized only after idea generation began and dipped during concept generation and selection ([Miller et al., 2019](1012)); it did not change idea counts but predicted idea goodness and selection of teammates' ideas ([Cole et al., 2020](1190)). Higher cognitive style scores went with more paradigm-breaking individual ideas ([Cole et al., 2021](866)).

6577|7861.text: Students and early-career graduate teams designed healthcare or healthy-living products in course projects, tracked through logs, surveys and coded sessions. Teams that prototyped early did better, while sheer amounts of sketching or time did not ([Elsen et al., 2012](739); [Häggman et al., 2013](783)). Psychological safety predicted idea goodness but not idea counts ([Cole et al., 2020](1190)).

6577|7868.text: Student studies use alternate-uses tasks with household objects as quick measures of fluency and flexibility, alone or next to engineering problems. Fluency and flexibility were strongly correlated between an alternate-uses test and an engineering ideation test [Johnson et al., 2015](953), and a scaled uses task lowered fluency and flexibility yet raised correctly scaled blade-reuse concepts afterward [Arabian & Shu, 2021](832). An online follow-up did not replicate an in-person conflict-processing benefit [Sahar & Shu, 2021](816).

6577|7874.text: Toys serve as the object in functional modeling, concept generation and design-course projects with student participants. In the most direct comparison, groups dissecting a Bumble Ball with component templates made fewer modeling mistakes and captured more functions and subsystems ([Abbott & Lough, 2008](444)). Other toy cases covered concept generator software ([Bryant et al., 2006](369)), collaborative sketching ([Chandrasegaran et al., 2014](1156)) and emotion during CAD edits ([Zhou et al., 2019](1079)).

6577|7876.text: Where students and vehicle problems meet, the vehicles are mostly engineering design tasks rather than brand or aesthetic judgments: an electric vehicle suspension, a pedestrian-safe bumper, a Lego vehicle and a paper bicycle. Studies were observational or course-based, tracking how novices sketch ([Radcliffe & Lee, 1994](1340)), what information they request ([Knoop, 1997](1703)), and where concepts are captured ([Yen et al., 1999](1623)). In [Knoop, 1997](1703), more communicated information went with better design quality.

6577|7877.text: Students generate or rate ideas for an alarm clock redesign, often alongside other problems, in controlled ideation experiments. Experiencing the product under impaired conditions led to more original concepts without lower technical quality ([Genco et al., 2011](610)), while just prompting students to think of nature gave no advantage ([Glier et al., 2012](672)). Metric profiles differed by problem and by familiarity ([Durand et al., 2015](949)), and the alarm clock and coconut problems behaved alike ([Levy et al., 2017](954)).

6577|7884.text: Students were asked for alternate uses or repurposing ideas for retired turbine blades, with a focus on getting the scale right. A visual-similarity method gave fewer concepts that were too small for the blade than human generation ([Kwon et al., 2018](927)), and a scaled uses task lowered fluency but raised correctly scaled blade ideas ([Arabian & Shu, 2021](832)). A memory recall induction made blade ideas more appropriate and feasible ([Arabian et al., 2020](1174)).

6577|7887.text: Cordless drills and related power tools appear only as course case objects in student studies of teaching tools and methods. Five students in a platform planning exercise on a power tool family gave preliminary efficiency results ([Sahin et al., 2006](535)), wiki groups dissecting products such as a cordless drill reported better product understanding than controls ([Devendorf et al., 2007](390)), and examiners agreed more on concrete product interactions than vague ones ([Tilstra et al., 2010](707)).

6577|7891.text: Students draw mental models of hair dryers, dissect them, or use them as objects for function analysis. Mental model scores improved after functional modeling instruction, significantly for the clothes dryer and vacuum, with a likely ceiling effect for the hair dryer ([Murphy et al., 2019](1004)), whereas a teardown left scores unchanged and worsened functional reasoning ([Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20)). Three function-analysis methods did not differ clearly ([Booth et al., 2013](762)).

6577|7897.text: Students work on the peanut sheller problem, mainly in controlled idea-generation experiments. Studies tested how teams share ideas ([Linsey et al., 2005](151)), how analogies from distant domains help ([Lopez et al., 2011](613)), and how examples cause fixation ([Fu et al., 2009](476)). Individuals outperformed collaborating teams on design quality ([Gyory et al., 2018](1011)), and one comparison found peanut and corn problems behaved alike ([Levy et al., 2017](954)).

6577|7901.text: The cardboard tower is a rapid prototyping task for engineering students. Students who built five early prototypes felt more time pressure but improved more between first and final towers ([Neeley et al., 2013](782)). Tool familiarity and self-efficacy shaped material choice and performance ([Menold et al., 2018](1092)), and perceived scarcity of time predicted perceived design performance ([Sibley et al., 2023](71)).

6577|7904.text: Container opener problems appear alongside assistive-device tasks in studies of method and cognition. Students designing a one-handed jar opener showed cognitive load that differed across stages and tracked idea uniqueness during ideation ([Calpin & Menold, 2022](893)). Problem framing predicted how paradigm-breaking solutions were, regardless of cognitive style fit ([Radwan et al., 2022](873)), and morphological analysis or TRIZ shifted effort toward behavior versus brainstorming ([Gero et al., 2012](728)).

6577|7908.text: Students designing a burrito-folding machine are used in controlled experiments on the aids given before concept generation. A chart with fewer functions and more means per function led to higher-rated concepts than a larger chart [Smith et al., 2006](538), and function-model users produced more concepts while interaction-model users produced higher-quality ones [Ramachandran et al., 2011](638). Non-functional requirements gave more and better concepts than functional ones [Worinkeng & Summers, 2014](1135).

6577|7915.text: The snow-insulation brief was used mostly with small student groups in think-aloud studies of word stimuli. Stimulus words given as verbs were often used as nouns, yet new ideas appeared more when they were used as verbs or modifiers ([Chiu & Shu, 2007](380)). Clashing stimuli led to more novel concepts ([Chiu & Shu, 2008](433)), but a later study found no gain in creativity from stimuli ([Chiu & Shu, 2010](641)).

6577|7918.text: Students cluster product elements (mixer, hair dryer, toilet) into subsystems from different representations in a shared paper task. Elements were more likely to be clustered when directly connected or physically close on the page [Patel et al., 2022](839), and representation effects were not consistent across products [Murphy et al., 2022](895). Cluster size was not correlated with design self-efficacy or need for closure [Patel et al., 2023](59).

6577|7935.text: Two groups of studies. In simulated smart-lock tasks, students trusted stereotype-congruent agents more in explicit behavior, such as a male voice in the office and a female voice at home ([Damen & Toh, 2017](1081)), but reaction-time measures showed no such difference ([Damen & Toh, 2018](1039)). The other pair, on team size and requirements, did not use the smart lock ([Nonso-Anyakwo & Summers, 2025](1437); [Nonso-Anyakwo & Summers, 2025](1439)).

6577|7939.text: Mugs and glasses serve as test objects in student studies of concept generation tools and preference, with small samples. A concept generator produced many viable thermal mug concepts beyond those students made manually ([Bryant et al., 2006](369)). Combining aggregate data with individual choices gave mugs best matching comfort perceptions ([Nandy & Goucher-Lambert, 2023](53)).

6577|7947.text: Student teams in an interdisciplinary bio-inspired design course are observed and then given methods to test. Observation described problem-driven and solution-driven routes with cross-domain analogies ([Vattam et al., 2010](609)) and found that finding biological sources online took longer than all downstream design activity ([Vattam & Goel, 2011](619)). Students applying the Four-Box method defined problems with about 86 percent accuracy and mostly commented positively ([Helms & Goel, 2014](1120)).

6577|7948.text: Students worked the bushing-pin alignment problem, usually with two other problems, to test language stimuli, mostly in small think-aloud studies. New ideas were introduced more when stimulus words were used as verbs or noun modifiers ([Chiu & Shu, 2007](380)), while stimuli did not raise concept creativity in a later experiment ([Chiu & Shu, 2010](641)). A separate word-association study had students describe peg fit in English or Telugu ([Mukerjee & Dabbeeru, 2010](646)).

6577|7949.text: Litter and trash collection briefs were given to students in ideation experiments, plus one protocol study of a train litter system. Handling an example grabber produced more fixation, and among those with an example, higher fixation went with lower originality ([Simmons et al., 2018](1078)). Group members generally improved the originality of initial litter-grabber ideas ([Blair & Hölttä-Otto, 2012](679)), and seven graduate students' protocols fit a design-process model ([Zeng, 2011](630)).

6577|7959.text: Students build or design robots, such as contest robots, sumo robots, and drones, in course projects and experiments. Outcome links are mixed. Early dimensioned drawings and prior fabrication experience went with better contest results, but sketch count did not ([Yang, 2003](296)). A prototyping method helped all ten teams hit a target ([Camburn et al., 2013](792)), while prototype cost was unrelated to outcome ([Nelson & Menold, 2020](1205)).

6577|7997.text: Engineering students solved the corn shucker brief in controlled experiments, usually alongside other problems, to test methods or compare problems. A plain prompt to think like nature gave no advantage ([Glier et al., 2012](672)), and participants rarely agreed on which thesaurus-found biology passages gave them ideas ([Glier et al., 2013](767)). Problem comparisons found peanut and corn problems behaved similarly ([Levy et al., 2017](954)), and problem familiarity influenced metrics ([Durand et al., 2015](949)).

6577|8018.text: Students work on consumer products such as toothbrushes and washing machines, mostly in experiments testing a method or tool. Results vary by intervention: a product-architecture representation gave more feasible mousetrap concepts ([Wie et al., 2003](287)), an inclusive-design scheme helped only to a limited extent ([Sangelkar & McAdams, 2013](772)), and dissection effects on novelty depended on personality ([Toh et al., 2012](727)). 6577|8032.text: Assembly in these studies is mostly virtual or CAD-based, with students adding mates, reviewing gearboxes or building from scrap-part models. Head-mounted VR improved error finding in gearbox reviews ([Casenave & Lugo, 2018](1082)), and in an immersive system navigation took 41 percent of activity ([Robinson et al., 2006](360)).

6577|8049.text: Students deal with mechanical parts, mechanisms and drawings as objects to interpret, modify or judge, using think-aloud, observation and some controlled experiments. Annotating a parametric CAD part with design intent led to better alteration choices ([Camba et al., 2014](1129)), while students with higher exam scores judged shaft similarity more by knowledge than by surface features ([Chaudhari et al., 2019](1087)). Mechanism-reading work compared novices with experts ([Waldron et al., 1989](1745)).

6577|8070.text: The spring-powered ball transporter was used mainly in ideation experiments that compared psychology volunteers' lab results with engineering students' design results. Incubation raised idea effectiveness in both settings and results correlated across them ([Shah et al., 2003](298)), though alignment was only 59 percent of cases in a larger run ([Shah et al., 2006](358)). Other ball tasks covered sketching versus building ([Faas et al., 2014](1133)) and graduate groups' written communication ([Jakiela & Orlikowski, 1991](1334)).

Teams with extreme Thinking-Feeling averages looked more creative in short ideation sessions ([Berthelsdorf & Stone, 2017](994)), mind-mapping partners acted as a catalyst for exploring ideas ([Chen et al., 2019](1063)), and mind-mapping gave wider problem statements than free writing ([Chen et al., 2021](840)). 6577|8219.text: Students work on syringes and a dialysis service model, mostly to test needs-finding and interviewing methods. 6577|8221.text: Sports equipment appears here as an incidental design problem rather than a unifying topic: students designed ball-moving devices and sports-themed products. Problem formulation patterns correlated with ideation outcomes for a basketball return device ([Dinar et al., 2015](929)), and analogy wording affected whether students used analogous products ([Linsey et al., 2007](379)).

6577|8224.text: Student studies use machinery-type problems, such as a plate-dipping mechanism, a laser welding device or a production line, to test evaluation, sketching and negotiation methods. Absolute ratings of concepts were more reliable than relative comparison ([Diteman & Stauffer, 1993](1505)), reinterpreting a sketch changed one student's whole concept ([Pache et al., 2001](197)), and a negotiation protocol led pairs to explore more alternatives ([Jin & Geslin, 2007](557)).

6577|8228.text: Precision instruments, here a low-cost atomic force microscope, appear in student ideation studies as the problem, with the third paper lacking details. Personality types differed in ideation results across brainstorming, mind-mapping and C-Sketch ([Choo et al., 2014](1134)). 6577|8230.text: Heuristic reasoning appears in engineering student studies as rules of thumb, estimation and method-choice strategies. 6577|8231.text: Students' estimation and quick judgment are tested in short exercises and group decisions.
