Effects are mixed across studies.

6577|8234.text: Memory appears as recall of prior knowledge, examples and analogies, mostly in student ideation experiments. Studies tested what students could recall or estimate ([Linder & Flowers, 1996](1733)), how the wording of memorized product descriptions shaped later analogy use ([Linsey et al., 2007](379)), and whether a memory-recall induction changed idea flexibility ([Arabian et al., 2020](1174)). Results are mixed, for example a teardown improved component identification but left mental model scores unchanged ([Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20)).

6577|8236.text: Student team studies treat shared understanding through communication, framing and goal awareness, using experiments, observation and surveys. A structured negotiation protocol led pairs to explore more alternatives and collaborate more efficiently ([Jin & Geslin, 2007](557)), teams followed a few common paths in framing a problem ([Hey et al., 2008](459)), and CAD teams saved calendar time but used more person-hours ([Cheng & Olechowski, 2021](854)).

6577|8237.text: Student teams and pairs were studied while generating ideas, mind-mapping or modeling together, through experiments and coded observation. Teammates' ideas raised idea counts and originality ([Linsey et al., 2005](151); [Blair & Hölttä-Otto, 2012](679)), and teammate stimulation tied to more novel concepts ([Sauder et al., 2013](769)). Results on team size and makeup are mixed: teams of three scored best in [Jacobs et al., 2019](1052).

6577|8238.text: Most studies are controlled experiments in which students ideate on everyday problems after seeing example solutions or other stimuli. Pictured examples led to strong fixation and lower originality ([Cardoso et al., 2009](525)), and a poor example slowed team convergence and lowered quality ([Fu et al., 2009](476)). Physical building showed no fixation in one study ([Viswanathan & Linsey, 2010](649)) but reduced novelty when model-making was costly ([Viswanathan & Linsey, 2011](608)).

6577|8239.text: Engineering students are the usual participants in divergent-thinking studies, from course-based concept tests to online uses-for-objects tasks. Some work validates measures: an eight-question test with fluency and flexibility scores ([Shah et al., 2010](661)), and strong links between alternate-uses and engineering ideation tests ([Johnson et al., 2015](953)). Others test interventions, such as TRIZ training improving novelty and variety ([Hernandez et al., 2012](676)); freshmen and upperclassmen did not differ in originality ([Bennetts et al., 2017](930)).

6577|8240.text: Prior knowledge appears here as fabrication experience, expertise, coursework or proficiency, usually as a predictor of design results in student experiments and course records. Prior fabrication experience correlated with better contest outcomes ([Yang, 2003](296)), novices fixated on examples as much as experts but produced fewer non-redundant ideas ([Viswanathan & Linsey, 2012](757)), coursework and project topics predicted project grades ([Ball & Lewis, 2019](1106)), and team scores followed the most proficient member ([Brownell et al., 2020](1186)).

6577|8241.text: Intrinsic motivation is not measured directly in these three studies, which instead vary the brief, setting or sketching conditions. Plain briefs gave high novelty but low appropriateness, while video examples did the reverse [Siang et al., 2018](939); a video game playlist gave the most creative ideas by self-report and pop the most ideas [Wojciechowski et al., 2025](1419). Novices' idea development appeared constrained by sketching [Radcliffe & Lee, 1994](1340).

6577|8246.text: Student studies typically give an inventory (KAI, Myers-Briggs, Big Five, creativity mode) before a project, then relate scores to idea novelty, selection or team results. Higher KAI went with more paradigm-breaking individual ideas ([Cole et al., 2021](866)), extraverts produced more novel ideas after dissection ([Toh et al., 2012](727)), and Wilde's model explained about 10% of capstone outcome variance ([Freiheit, 2014](1149)).

6577|8247.text: Student studies of evaluative judgment ask how reliably and validly students rate ideas, designs or sketches. One of three design-quality scales gave unreliable ratings across sessions [Hyde & Stauffer, 1990](1393), and rarity-based and perceived novelty ratings showed only moderate agreement [Weaver et al., 2019](940). Novice raters with high mutual agreement, especially after training, produced composite originality ratings close to experts' [Green et al., 2014](1131), while risk-averse students chose less creative ideas [Toh & Miller, 2014](1142).

6577|8248.text: Students were observed or tested as they framed problems, using think-aloud protocols, problem maps, brief variations and requirement-writing exercises. Problem maps showed an expert attending to more attributes and relations than a novice ([Dinar et al., 2011](636)), and map patterns correlated with later ideation ([Dinar et al., 2015](929)). Mind-mapping gave wider-ranging problem statements ([Chen et al., 2021](840)), and brief content shifted novelty against usability ([Siang et al., 2018](939)).

6577|8249.text: The papers link flexibility to students' ideation, mainly through interventions, brain activity and search behavior rather than a direct flexibility test. Teaming and problem framing changed idea quality compared with neutral ideation, but design heuristic cards did not [Henderson et al., 2018](923). Brainstorming produced an early left prefrontal response that was not sustained, unlike morphological analysis and TRIZ [Shealy et al., 2018](1047), and students met more unexpected search results than professionals [Kwon et al., 2022](833).

6577|8250.text: Student participants had emotions read from facial video, mood words in reflections or self-rated experience, across CAD work, sketching warm-ups and team projects. Paired CAD users showed more emotion than solo users ([Zhou et al., 2019](1079)); team mood shifted over a project but individual mood did not ([Harris & Toh, 2023](23)); divergent team mood went with lower grades ([Harris & Toh, 2024](24)). Warm-ups reduced stress without changing idea counts ([Hu et al., 2015](945)).

6577|8251.text: Engineering students' social influence is studied through team behavior in course projects, using sensors, video coding, surveys and simulation. Sociometric badges captured total speaking time accurately but missed precise speaking moments ([Chen & Miller, 2017](1002)). Leadership coded from video was shared across members ([Righter et al., 2019](1044)), and virtual teams reported higher perceived influence than face-to-face teams ([Singh et al., 2021](846)).

6577|8252.text: Students took part in studies on understanding users, using simulated impairment, extreme-user tools, drawing people into sketches, or inferring a driver's thoughts. Experiencing a product under impairment gave more original concepts ([Genco et al., 2011](610)), and guided empathy tools captured a wider range of latent needs than unguided ones ([Raviselvam et al., 2018](959)). GPT-4 matched designers at inferring user goals in [Zhu et al., 2024](85).

6577|8254.text: Student studies examine reasoning through think-aloud protocols, coded behavior or controlled experiments on design and drawing-reading tasks. Findings depend on the kind of reasoning: experts and students differed in forward versus inverse reasoning ([Waldron et al., 1989](1745)), iteration was far higher on a creative problem than a routine one ([Chuslip & Jin, 2004](576)), and an imposed search strategy improved results ([Egan et al., 2014](1139)). A teardown improved component identification but worsened functional reasoning ([Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20)).

6577|8255.text: Engineering students are the usual participants when mental models are drawn out or shaped through representations and instruction. Graduate students' functional mental-model scores rose after functional-modeling instruction ([Murphy et al., 2019](1004)), but a hair-dryer teardown left scores unchanged ([Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20)). Representation shaped understanding too: system-behavior models helped with causal questions while diagrams helped spatial ones ([Helms et al., 2010](605)), and physical building raised the share of functional ideas ([Viswanathan & Linsey, 2010](649)).

6577|8256.text: Engineering students' trust is studied in simulations and AI-assisted design tasks. Students trusted a simulated smart lock more when the agent's gender matched a stereotype for its setting ([Damen & Toh, 2017](1081)), though reaction time showed no such effect ([Damen & Toh, 2018](1039)). With AI suggestions on truss problems, confidence in the AI fell after poor performance but not good ([Chong et al., 2022](845)).

6577|8257.text: Students used biological descriptions, patents, example products or word stimuli to generate concepts in design-by-analogy experiments. Results vary with presentation: general product wording helped later analogy use ([Linsey et al., 2007](379)), near analogies gave higher quality but far ones less novel best concepts ([Fu et al., 2012](755)), and a plain nature prompt gave no gain ([Glier et al., 2012](672)).

6577|8259.text: Students are the participants in studies that measured mental effort directly or used it to interpret task differences, during sketching, ideating or modeling. Workload (NASA-TLX) differed across ideation and prototyping, with mental demand tied to idea quality only in ideation ([Calpin & Menold, 2022](893)). Facilitation lowered perceived load ([Murphy et al., 2023](50)), but nominal-team managers carried heavier burden ([Gyory et al., 2022](851)).

6577|8261.text: Planning, strategy and cognitive control show up here in student design projects, studied through design journals, think-aloud protocols and, in two studies, prefrontal brain imaging. System-level idea generation and refinement best predicted design quality ([Wilkening & Sobek, 2004](325)), and experts followed a similar strategy while treating checking as secondary ([Motte et al., 2004](582)). Prefrontal activation differed across TRIZ steps ([Milovanovic et al., 2021](826)) and was lower when students used ChatGPT ([Aruon et al., 2025](1460)).

6577|8265.text: Student team studies link composition, personality or communication patterns to team outcomes, using course projects, surveys and message logs. Constraining team composition by personality preference raised the share of prize-winning teams from 29 to 60 percent [Wilde, 1997](1694), though Wilde's model explained about 10% of variance in capstone outcomes [Freiheit, 2014](1149). Stronger teams used emojis more and had lower average member centrality [Olechowski et al., 2020](1202).

6577|8267.text: Engineering students' learning appears in course-based studies using dissection, software, games and goal-setting. Multimedia motor software raised pre/post scores ([Reamon & Sheppard, 1999](1626)), and a multiplayer game left all participants competent at system-level heuristics ([Topcu et al., 2025](1432)). Goal framing showed a trade-off: learning goals raised test scores while performance goals produced better designs ([Chaudhari et al., 2021](908)). Dissection results varied, with a teardown improving component identification but not mental-model scores ([Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20)).

6577|8270.text: Student studies bring up satisficing mostly through stopping, search and selection decisions. Students stopped searching based on thresholds for target quality, resources spent and improvement sought, which shifted with how competitive they judged an opponent [Shergadwala & Panchal, 2020](1179). Users told to follow a univariate-then-local search did significantly better than those without a strategy [Egan et al., 2014](1139), and stated reasoning did not predict actions or results in concept selection [Mirabito & Goucher-Lambert, 2021](876).

6577|8271.text: No paper here measures social loafing directly; students appear in group-versus-individual and team-process studies. Nominal teams of five working alone produced higher-quality designs than collaborating teams [Gyory et al., 2018](1011), and a free-rider game with grade payoffs and 40 rounds led to the most mutual contribution [Veluru & Takai, 2006](537). Systematic procedures seemed to encourage more equal participation in a small group-design system study [McMahon, 1991](1367).

6577|8272.text: Goal orientation appears with student teams and individuals in a few differing ways. Learning goals raised learning-test scores while performance goals produced better designs ([Chaudhari et al., 2021](908)). Requirement-style goals led to longer persistence and higher scores than maximize-the-merit framing ([Malak et al., 2022](863)). One exploratory study found possible links between goal orientation and function-modeling behavior, turned into hypotheses ([Patel & Summers, 2021](874)).

6577|8274.text: Students were usually given a lottery or risk survey and then asked to generate, choose or advance design concepts. More risk-averse students generated and selected less creative milk-frother ideas ([Toh & Miller, 2014](1142)), yet risk attitude did not predict prototype choices ([Starkey et al., 2018](1097)). Choice-inferred risk attitudes predicted strategic decisions better than the questionnaire ([Avşar et al., 2022](865)).

6577|8275.text: Students complete risk questionnaires or lottery tasks, which are sometimes linked to what they do in a design task. Risk-averse students generated and selected less creative ideas ([Toh & Miller, 2014](1142)). Attitudes inferred from students' design choices predicted strategic decisions far better than questionnaire scores, suggesting risk attitude is contextual ([Avşar et al., 2022](865)), and a new engineering-specific test was reliable overall, though its domains were questioned ([Bossuyt et al., 2011](678)).

6577|8276.text: Psychological safety is surveyed in student design teams, mostly first-year engineering courses, often at several time points. Team safety varied widely across teams and dipped during concept generation and selection ([Miller et al., 2019](1012)). Safety predicted idea goodness but not idea count ([Cole et al., 2020](1190)); women felt safer with women ([Cole et al., 2022](857)); turn-taking predicted individual safety ([O’Connell et al., 2022](861)); capstone safety was stable over two semesters ([Arpini-Lorenzoni et al., 2024](3)).

6577|8277.text: Engineering students solve constrained design problems such as trusses, parameter tuning and concept generation while researchers track how they search. Top parameter-tuning performers resembled a well-tuned simulated annealing algorithm, while the worst were near random ([Yu et al., 2015](1037)). High-performing truss teams chose simpler designs and explored small regions thoroughly ([McComb et al., 2014](1148)); integrated optimization tools gave better designs faster ([Burnell et al., 2017](1022)); team size effects varied ([Jacobs et al., 2019](1052)).

6577|8279.text: Student participants state or rate preferences in several settings, and the studies show preferences shifting with context. A design team's assessment of the same carafe attribute changed substantially over time ([Honda et al., 2010](642)). Showing environmental impact reduced the value placed on product form and raised function ([Goucher-Lambert & Cagan, 2014](1122)). Preferences for CAD models were inconsistent with preferences for physical eyeglass frames ([Echerd et al., 2023](18)).

6577|8280.text: Studies of engineering students on schema activation mostly look at how prior knowledge and representations shape what students see and group. Students clustered product elements differently depending on layout and representation type ([Patel et al., 2022](839); [Murphy et al., 2022](895)), and those with higher exam scores leaned more on knowledge than surface features when judging design similarity ([Chaudhari et al., 2019](1087)). A teardown improved component identification but left mental-model scores unchanged ([Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20)).

6577|8281.text: Self-efficacy is usually a survey measure collected alongside a design task, such as ideation, tower building or truss decisions, and sometimes as a course outcome. A bioinspired design course was followed by higher design confidence and lower anxiety ([Durand et al., 2015](917)). Elsewhere it was linked to material choice and tower performance ([Menold et al., 2018](1092)), but not to how students clustered system elements ([Patel et al., 2023](59)).

6577|8289.text: Aesthetic preference is gathered from mostly student participants by ratings or choices on shapes. Preference for wheel rims was predicted best by Gestalt variables combined with attached meaning and emotion ([Lugo et al., 2012](708)). An interactive genetic algorithm converged on small problems and showed shared and individual trends for an elegant glass ([Poirson et al., 2011](706)). Combining aggregate data with individuals' own choices best matched personal comfort perceptions of mugs ([Nandy & Goucher-Lambert, 2023](53)).

6577|8291.text: Student reflection appears in three quite different settings: a course with reflective reports, a textbook reading study, and an experiment on redesigned design tools. Reflective reports gave strong evidence of learning about concurrency ([Radcliffe, 1996](1731)), and a redesigned Pugh tool prompted deeper responses on social factors ([Waggoner et al., 2025](1444)). Learning from a text was active ([Sheppard et al., 1998](1656)).

6577|8294.text: Affective appraisal appears as liking, preference, or satisfaction ratings from students. Preference for wheel rims was predicted best by Gestalt variables combined with users' attached meaning and emotion ([Lugo et al., 2012](708)). Combining aggregate data with each person's choices gave mug designs best aligned with individual comfort perceptions ([Nandy & Goucher-Lambert, 2023](53)). Students who built five early prototypes felt less satisfied with them yet improved more ([Neeley et al., 2013](782)).

6577|8297.text: Students were studied handling information while designing, through think-aloud, concept-mapping and survey work, using small observational samples. Two students designing a bicycle lock generated most information themselves rather than accessing it ([Baya & Leifer, 1994](1506)), and students built concept maps in bursts of elements ([Kochenberger & Sen, 2023](34)). A packaging study found larger fonts gave fastest selection, though participants preferred other designs ([Cho et al., 2014](1154)).

6577|8298.text: Incubation is tested by inserting a break or unrelated activity into an ideation or design-exploration session and comparing performance afterward. Breaks improved idea effectiveness in both psychology-lab and engineering-design runs ([Shah et al., 2003](298); [Shah et al., 2006](358)), and a break improved AI-assisted satellite design more than reflection did ([Song et al., 2023](74)). Distantly related information helped only when given during a break ([Tseng et al., 2008](458)).

6577|8302.text: Student experiments compare interacting teams with individuals or look at whose designs get adopted; conformity itself is not tested directly. Teams that did not interact and used their best member's solution did best ([McComb et al., 2017](986)), nominal teams beat collaborating teams ([Gyory et al., 2018](1011)), and team performance followed the strongest member, whose simpler designs teammates adopted ([Brownell et al., 2020](1186)).

6577|8309.text: Engineering students sketched, mapped concepts or brainstormed while researchers inferred memory-related processes from pen pauses or brain sensing, in small observational studies. Most objects in a student sketch were drawn in one pen-stroke cluster, read as chunking ([Sen et al., 2017](1046)), and concept maps grew in bursts ([Kochenberger & Sen, 2023](34)). Prefrontal activation differed across ideation methods ([Shealy et al., 2018](1047)).

6577|8310.text: Student studies touch transfer indirectly, through learning activities. [Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20) found no change in mental model scores after a teardown, so no transfer was seen, with better component identification but worse functional reasoning. Course studies reported students using formal knowledge during hardware work ([Brereton et al., 1993](1516)) and rarely reusing past design archives ([Liang et al., 1998](1648)).

6577|8317.text: Studies pair students with hands-on activities such as building, simulation, prototyping or makerspace work, and look for learning mainly through observation, reflection or interview. The pair using simulation software used all four Kolb learning modes, against two for the paper-only pair ([Reamon & Sheppard, 1997](1695)), early rapid prototyping went with larger improvement but more time pressure ([Neeley et al., 2013](782)), and action patterns suggested students drew inspiration from objects they handled ([Hess & Summers, 2014](1146)).

6577|8328.text: Insight appears in student studies mainly as recognizing latent needs or reframing a problem. Empathy tools and extreme-user perspectives helped students identify latent needs ([Raviselvam et al., 2018](959); [Raviselvam et al., 2019](952)). Problem framing significantly predicted how paradigm-breaking students' solutions were, whether or not the frame matched their cognitive style ([Radwan et al., 2022](873)), and modeling function changed how students defined it ([Patel et al., 2020](1206)).

6577|8332.text: Priming appears in student experiments that expose participants to a stimulus, such as words, collages, or example information, before ideation. Collage priming increased sustainability-signaling features ([She & MacDonald, 2012](690)) and eco-friendly ideas, though not social or economic ones ([Liao & MacDonald, 2018](1111)). Clashing word stimuli produced more novel concepts ([Chiu & Shu, 2008](433)). Distant information shaped solutions only when given mid-task ([Tseng et al., 2008](458)).

6577|8341.text: Students' sketches, diagrams and physical builds are examined as outside aids to thinking, mostly in course settings. Sketch volume tracked outcome later in a project, and journal sketch counts correlated with class grade ([Song & Agogino, 2004](330)), while sketching first did not change ball-lifting performance versus building directly ([Faas et al., 2014](1133)). An inclusive-design diagram helped only to a limited extent ([Sangelkar & McAdams, 2013](772)), and ChatGPT use lowered brain-measured effort ([Aruon et al., 2025](1460)).

6577|8343.text: None of these papers measure overconfidence directly, so the link is loose. They involve students making design decisions in teams, where one course project showed students beginning to see how individual knowledge falls short in system-level choices ([Fujita, 2002](238)), and a pilot recorded decision traps in group discussion ([Nichols & Olewnik, 2012](726)). Non-interacting teams did best on one task ([McComb et al., 2017](986)).

6577|8367.text: Students were compared with experts, or studied for traits of expertise, mostly through think-aloud and observation on drawings, idea generation and design activity. Experts reasoned backward from overall function while novices focused on geometry ([Chovan & Waldron, 1990](1337)), and an experienced designer produced most ideas by analogy while a student fixated ([Shah et al., 1993](1522)). Capstone outcomes tracked how time was spent ([Wilkening & Sobek, 2004](325)).

6577|8461.text: Two strands appear: course studies that train or test spatial skills, and studies relating sketching or visual representation to design work. Spatial test scores rose over a semester, mostly after sketching instruction rather than CAD ([Hilton et al., 2018](1101)), and with no clear effect of visualization medium ([Zorn & Gericke, 2020](1196)). Sketching ability showed no notable link to design outcome ([Cham & Yang, 2005](153)), while head-mounted VR improved assembly error finding ([Casenave & Lugo, 2018](1082)).

6577|8521.text: Engineering students' risk and ambiguity attitudes are measured with lottery surveys and linked to creative concept choices. More risk-averse students generated and chose less creative ideas, and generating creative ideas did not predict choosing them ([Toh & Miller, 2014](1142)). In a later study, risk aversion did not predict choices, and students favored medium uniqueness with high usefulness ([Starkey et al., 2018](1097)). Cluster sizes were unrelated to need for closure ([Patel et al., 2023](59)).

6577|8522.text: Student studies touch implicit cognition indirectly, mostly through tacit knowledge in varied tasks. Over half of one student team's design noun phrases appeared in informal audio and video, only 5 percent in formal reports [Yen et al., 1999](1623). Making team knowledge explicit did not raise innovativeness but reduced errors [Petrovic et al., 2006](356), and students assumed an unspecified user was a man [Schauer et al., 2023](69).

6577|8523.text: The papers are varied, and attention shows up mostly through where students look or what they notice. Eye tracking and gaze maps were used in a diagram-recognition study, where attention went to dense clusters at object interfaces ([Fuge & Kara, 2009](497)), and in an eyeglass-preference study ([Echerd et al., 2023](18)). Others used EEG or skin response while sketching ([Hu et al., 2015](945)), or looked at how students attended to users ([Trivedi et al., 2025](1434)).

6577|8524.text: Most studies look at bias in how students choose among ideas or interpret users, mainly ownership bias. Male students chose more of their own ideas when rating teammates' ([Toh et al., 2015](925)), and priming shifted the bias ([Liao & MacDonald, 2018](1111)). Students also assumed an unspecified user was a man ([Schauer et al., 2023](69)). Team safety predicted how often teammates' ideas were picked ([Cole et al., 2020](1190)).

6577|8528.text: Engineering students appear in studies of how design knowledge is represented, whether in function models, problem maps or similarity judgments. Three function-analysis methods showed no clear differences for novices ([Booth et al., 2013](762)), while students whose definitions stressed input/output and process built larger function models ([Patel et al., 2020](1206)). Problem-map patterns correlated with ideation outcomes ([Dinar et al., 2015](929)), and human and computed similarity agreed mainly on clearly dissimilar items ([Kwon & Goucher-Lambert, 2023](35)).

6578|6600.text: Non-expert participants generate or revise ideas in workshops or online tasks after a manipulation. Personal connection to a simulated population changed how much the simulation boosted creativity and empathy ([Raviselvam et al., 2017](950)), gratitude did not change Alternate Uses scores and gave only tentative support in blade repurposing ([Sisson et al., 2021](830)), and a chatbot assistant earned more trust when it performed well or behaved empathetically ([Renji & Liao, 2025](1454)).

6578|6603.text: Lay users and non-users are interviewed, often alongside ratings or diaries, to draw out product needs. Disabled phone users shared ordinary users' needs and voiced extra ones ([Hannukainen & Hölttä-Otto, 2006](366)), robot-vacuum non-users gave more extensive reasons and so more customer attributes ([Augustin et al., 2021](888)), and customers preferred different products in different usage contexts ([Green et al., 2005](142)).

6578|6604.text: General-public samples, often online panel or Mechanical Turk respondents, answer rating or choice questionnaires about products such as vehicles, solar panels and dashboard displays. Preferences depended on context: solar panel appearance preferences shifted when panels were shown on roofs [Bao et al., 2014](1162), and perceived vehicle safety varied with personal traits, with shape ranked most influential [Cai et al., 2019](1071). Drivers preferred an animated coffee-cup display for smoother driving [Potvin-Bernal & Shu, 2019](1098).

6578|6607.text: Alternate-uses tasks (paperclip, spoon, everyday objects) are given to broad participant pools, including several hundred people from mixed backgrounds. Later responses were more original than early ones, and longer, more elaborate answers went with lower originality and fluency ([Dippo & Kudrowitz, 2015](933)). Naming new uses went with looking at multiple object views in an eye-tracking study ([Kwon et al., 2019](956)), and a gratitude induction did not change scores ([Sisson et al., 2021](830)).

6578|6611.text: Members of the general public, often crowd workers, rate or rank products, sketches and concepts. Studies model individual preferences from choices ([Orsborn et al., 2008](457)), test how sketch finish shifts liking ([Macomber & Yang, 2011](718)), and show sketch quality inflating idea ratings ([Kwon & Kudrowitz, 2019](928)). Presentation medium also matters: immersive VR gave higher trust and risk ratings than video, though behavior rankings matched ([Islam et al., 2024](26)).

6578|6616.text: Members of the general public are interviewed about product use and needs, often alongside other measures. Participants were interviewed while cooking, with failure modes derived from energy use ([Withanage et al., 2014](1123)); taxonomy-guided focus groups elicited more customer requirements than traditional ones ([Hauge & Stauffer, 1993](1588)). LLM personas answering the same interview questions reproduced general needs but missed deeper cultural themes ([Das et al., 2025](1453)).

6578|6617.text: Lay participants, usually online, compare pairs of products, forms or image sets by appearance, emotion, function or variety. Preferences between solar panel images changed when the panels were shown on roofs instead of standalone ([Bao et al., 2014](1162)). Emotional ratings of coarse car abstractions matched ratings of the final models ([Orbay et al., 2013](768)), and functional similarity judgments took more effort but were more accurate than appearance ones ([Asuzu et al., 2025](1431)).

6578|6619.text: The link is loose: the general-public samples in these papers mostly rate, choose or describe things, with written reflection a minor component. Participants in art-based workshops wrote and drew about environmental attitudes before later rating eco-feedback sketches, and attitude shaped their emotional reactions [Wilson et al., 2024](82). A related online study found labeling helmet concepts as AI or human generated had no effect on evaluation [Mirabito et al., 2025](1438).

6578|6726.text: Lay participants use or simulate using a product, such as a faucet, voice assistant or kitchen tool, while researchers log behavior, water use or stated needs. A hidden-operator faucet cut water use 26.5 percent ([Jou et al., 2019](1104)), and slow sink drainage cut it about 14% ([Halabieh & Shu, 2021](808)). A disability simulation suit gave comparable needs but slowed dexterity more than real disabilities ([Armstrong et al., 2015](1088)).

6578|6824.text: General-public participants judge approaching autonomous vehicles in online images or VR, then rate trust, safety or risk. Earlier display of a yielding message raised crossing, trust and perceived safety, while dynamic speed raised trust and safety but not crossing [She et al., 2021](903), and advisory messages raised trust depending on the expected decision [She, 2020](1201). VR gave higher trust and risk ratings than video with equal comprehensibility [Islam et al., 2024](26).

6578|7876.text: Online and in-person general-public participants rate, rank or choose among car images, silhouettes or sounds, often adding eye tracking or fMRI. Individual utility functions predicted preferred vehicle fronts well, with high-utility designs picked 78 percent of the time [Orsborn et al., 2008](457), and emotional responses to coarse car abstractions closely matched those to full models [Orbay et al., 2013](768). Brand recognition depended strongly on the manufacturer [Burnap et al., 2015](1091).

6578|7903.text: Online general-public samples respond to pedestrian-crossing scenarios with autonomous vehicles, not the walking-and-texting brief. Advisory messages raised trust when crossing was expected ([She, 2020](1201)). Showing the yielding message earlier raised crossing, trust, and perceived safety ([She et al., 2021](903)). Immersive VR gave higher trust and risk ratings than video, though the relative effect of vehicle behaviors was the same ([Islam et al., 2024](26)).

6578|8018.text: These studies recruit non-specialist people, often online, to react to everyday products such as blenders, coffee presses, dispensers and wearables, mostly through surveys, ratings and interviews. They find what people prefer or notice: viewers recalled material, shape and function from sketches ([Sagan & Yang, 2012](743)), and preferences shifted with usage context ([Green et al., 2005](142)). Product-based nudges for sustainable behavior gave mixed results ([Saadi & Yang, 2020](1183)).

6578|8231.text: Lay participants judged vehicles, carafes and product ideas from images, and the studies show how cues such as form or sketch quality shape judgments. Perceived environmental friendliness could be modeled from vehicle silhouette features [Reid et al., 2009](486), and sketch quality strongly influenced ratings of an idea's value [Kwon & Kudrowitz, 2019](928). Representation mattered for preferences but inference questions were unaffected [Reid et al., 2012](741).

6578|8233.text: Lay participants reflected on or judged their own behavior and needs in three studies, rather than a shared metacognition task. In a living-lab kitchen, participants cooked, were interviewed and tried to cut energy use, yielding failure modes of overconsumption ([Withanage et al., 2014](1123)). Older adults' self-rated standing difficulty did not track therapist ratings ([Stansfield et al., 2023](76)), and pedestrians rated confidence and trust in autonomous vehicle messages ([She, 2020](1201)).

6578|8234.text: Members of the public, and some professionals and students, generated or described things from memory in short tasks. Longer, more elaborate answers on a paperclip uses test went with lower originality and fluency under time limits ([Dippo & Kudrowitz, 2015](933)). 6600|7884.text: Concept generation here means alternate-use ideation for retired wind-turbine blades, tested with student samples. An episodic memory induction raised flexibility and made blade ideas more feasible and appropriate, though not more fluent ([Arabian et al., 2020](1174)). A scaled uses task lowered fluency but raised correctly scaled blade ideas ([Arabian & Shu, 2021](832)), and gratitude gave only tentative support ([Sisson et al., 2021](830)).

6600|7897.text: The peanut sheller is a common concept generation problem, used mostly with engineering students in controlled experiments. Rotating ideas among teammates gave more ideas ([Linsey et al., 2005](151)), WordTree analogy search found more analogies without changing idea count ([Linsey et al., 2008](440)), and a poor example slowed team convergence ([Fu et al., 2009](476)). Individuals outperformed teams on quality in [Gyory et al., 2018](1011).

6600|7903.text: The walking-and-texting accident problem is a shared brief for ideation studies with students and professional designers. Studies found designers structure information in clusters, relations and nests [Toh & Damen, 2020](1197), that real-time near or far stimuli shaped final innovativeness through the stimulus's own innovativeness more than its distance [Goucher-Lambert et al., 2019](944), and that human facilitation changed team behavior versus an assistant [Maier et al., 2020](1210).

6600|7908.text: The burrito-folding machine is a shared brief in controlled experiments where students generated concepts under different aids, usually morphological charts, function models or requirement sets. A chart with fewer functions and more means gave higher-rated concepts ([Smith et al., 2006](538)); function models gave more concepts while interaction models gave higher quality ([Ramachandran et al., 2011](638)); and non-functional requirements beat functional ones on quantity and quality ([Worinkeng & Summers, 2014](1135)).

6600|7915.text: The snow-insulation brief mostly appears in think-aloud studies in which students generate concepts from stimulus words. Clashing words were used more often as verbs and gave more novel concepts ([Chiu & Shu, 2008](433)), but a later study with similar, opposite or no stimulus words found no gain in concept creativity ([Chiu & Shu, 2010](641)). Related snow problems also supported iteration analysis ([Chuslip & Jin, 2004](576)) and variety-metric comparison ([Henderson et al., 2017](922)).

6600|7949.text: The litter collection brief appears in student studies, two controlled experiments and one protocol study, where participants generated concepts for litter grabbers or train litter disposal. The rest of a group generally improved originality of the initial idea ([Blair & Hölttä-Otto, 2012](679)), and handling an example product increased fixation, with higher fixation tied to lower originality, especially for seniors ([Simmons et al., 2018](1078)). All seven protocols fit an environment-based design process ([Zeng, 2011](630)).

6600|7959.text: Participants generate robot concepts with stimuli such as patents, cards or design principles. Closer patents were used more and gave higher quality concepts, while more distant ones gave more novel concepts ([Venkataraman et al., 2017](934)); concepts made with design cards were rated higher in quality and novelty ([Kalimuthu et al., 2022](823)); originality was higher on a novel problem regardless of expertise ([Tan et al., 2022](825)).

6600|7997.text: The corn shucker is a recurring concept generation prompt in studies of ideation methods and problem choice. Telling students to consider how nature would solve the problem gave no significant advantage ([Glier et al., 2012](672)), and problems differed in their metric profiles ([Durand et al., 2015](949)). Telling students their sketching would be evaluated barely affected idea quantity ([Weaver et al., 2022](841)).

6600|8018.text: The shared studies have people generate ideas for everyday consumer products such as mousetraps, toothbrushes, packaging and smartphone stands, rather than analyzing written user comments. A new architecture representation raised feasibility and detail but not originality ([Wie et al., 2003](287)), dissection raised novelty mainly for extraverts ([Toh et al., 2012](727)), and tools changed sketch quality more than quantity ([Das et al., 2022](813)).

6600|8054.text: The furniture-layout link is thin, and the papers mostly concern furniture or products in a broad sense. One protocol study had a graduate student arrange beds and a desk in a bedroom, with EEG showing more visual-thinking effort during solution generation than evaluation ([Nguyen & Zeng, 2010](639)). Others involve novices' sketching ([Radcliffe & Lee, 1994](1340)) and AI-generated office chairs ([Song et al., 2025](1415)).

6600|8218.text: The file does not give clear examples of technology-push prompts; the shared papers mostly ask students to generate ideas under varied conditions. Incubation raised idea effectiveness in both lab and design experiments, and results correlated across the two levels [Shah et al., 2003](298); later work found suspending judgment raised quality but cut quantity [Shah et al., 2006](358). Team personality averages related to creativity differently by method [Berthelsdorf & Stone, 2017](994).

6600|8221.text: Sports equipment appears as the target in idea-generation studies, such as ball-moving and basketball-return devices. Designers started with common solution categories and moved to novel ones, with example timing mattering more than commonness ([Perttula & Liikkanen, 2006](361)). Problem-map patterns from a basketball-return task predicted ideation variety and quality better than novelty ([Dinar et al., 2015](929)). A playground study documented decision traps ([Nichols & Olewnik, 2012](726)).

6600|8233.text: Concept generation studies relate to metacognition only indirectly, through interventions that prompted students to reflect on or monitor their ideas, within course and lab experiments. Naming and rating task aspects did not raise innovativeness but reduced errors ([Petrovic et al., 2006](356)), and classifying one's own ideas raised novelty more than combining them ([Kirjavainen & Hölttä-Otto, 2019](924)). A short lesson on sketching changed sketch content but lowered sketch counts ([Ruocco et al., 2009](498)).

6600|8234.text: Most studies have students generate ideas after reading information, seeing examples or working with a partner, and treat recall of what they saw or read as part of the process. Novices' recalled information resembled the language of their ideas ([Mertens & Toh, 2019](1048)), and a recall induction made alternate uses more flexible and elaborate without changing fluency ([Arabian et al., 2020](1174)). Others touch memory only indirectly ([Chuslip & Jin, 2004](576)).

6600|8237.text: Group concept generation is studied mostly with student teams in experiments, plus a few observational and professional-team studies. Seeing teammates' ideas raised idea counts and originality ([Linsey et al., 2005](151); [Blair & Hölttä-Otto, 2012](679)), and seeding or correcting by a partner went with more novel concepts ([Sauder et al., 2013](769)). A poor example slowed convergence ([Fu et al., 2009](476)).

6600|8238.text: Studies pair idea generation with fixation mostly through experiments that show designers an example and check how closely ideas copy it. A pictured book-grabbing device produced strong fixation and lower originality whether drawn or photographed [Cardoso et al., 2009](525), and a poor example slowed team convergence and lowered quality [Fu et al., 2009](476). Results vary: physical modeling lowered novelty only when building was costly [Viswanathan & Linsey, 2011](608).

6600|8239.text: Studies mostly ask students to produce ideas for everyday or engineering problems, then score fluency, flexibility, novelty or variety, often while varying a method, stimulus or mood. TRIZ lectures raised novelty and variety ([Hernandez et al., 2012](676)), and a recall induction improved flexibility but not fluency ([Arabian et al., 2020](1174)). Only the Alternative Uses Test predicted expert-rated creative ideas ([Kwon et al., 2017](914)).

6600|8240.text: Domain knowledge shows up indirectly in these ideation studies, through expertise, familiarity or structured aids. Experts and novices fixated on example features equally, but only experts benefited from alternate problem representations ([Viswanathan & Linsey, 2012](757)). Interest strengthened and familiarity weakened the link between divergent-thinking scores and creative bicycle ideas ([Kwon et al., 2017](914)), and structured sustainability guidance changed design decisions for novices and graduates alike ([Ross et al., 2019](1102)).

6600|8241.text: Motivation and interest are self-rated or measured next to idea generation tasks. Self-rated motivation predicted novelty with one method but few other factors mattered ([Moreno et al., 2015](957)); interest strengthened, and familiarity weakened, the link between divergent-thinking scores and expert-rated creative ideas ([Kwon et al., 2017](914)); and participants preferred a pop playlist, while a video game playlist gave the most creative ideas by self-report ([Wojciechowski et al., 2025](1419)).

6600|8246.text: Studies pair ideation with cognitive style by measuring style (often the KAI inventory or creativity-mode tests) and relating it to ideas or team behavior. A broad-search style correlated with novelty and a detail-search style with quality [Weaver et al., 2018](931), and higher KAI went with a greater chance of paradigm-breaking individual ideas [Cole et al., 2021](866). Effects were smaller elsewhere: style had small effects on concept screening [Heininger et al., 2018](1035).

6600|8248.text: Studies combine ideation with problem framing by varying what designers know or write about the problem. Plain briefs gave high novelty but low appropriateness, while video examples did the reverse [Siang et al., 2018](939), and mind-mapping gave more systematic problem exploration than free writing [Chen et al., 2021](840). Designers iterated far more, including redefining the problem, on a creative problem than a routine one [Chuslip & Jin, 2004](576).

6600|8249.text: Flexibility is approached through idea variety, interventions and brain activation during idea generation. Incubation helped consistently while suspending judgment raised quality but cut quantity ([Shah et al., 2006](358)); idea quality differed with teaming and problem framing but not with heuristic cards ([Henderson et al., 2018](923)); and brainstorming gave an early left prefrontal response that was not sustained, unlike morphological analysis and TRIZ ([Shealy et al., 2018](1047)).

6600|8250.text: Affective measures in concept generation studies are physiological or self-reported and track stress, engagement or trust. Warm-ups reduced stress during sketching, and art warm-ups raised engagement for younger participants, without changing idea counts ([Hu et al., 2015](945)). Empathetic chatbot behavior raised trust and improved perceived effort and enjoyment ([Renji & Liao, 2025](1454)). One study with an evaluation instruction found negligible effect on productivity ([Weaver et al., 2022](841)).

6600|8252.text: Empathy is studied in concept generation by directing students toward users, stakeholders or contextual requirements. Drawing people in sketches led to deeper reflections on users and fewer claims that a design suits everyone ([Makhlouf et al., 2023](43)). Scrum-story requirements raised novelty of solution fragments without hurting sketch quantity ([Patel et al., 2021](864)), and participants varied from dismissing to integrating stakeholder input ([Stancliff et al., 2025](1446)).

6600|8254.text: Studies combine ideation with reasoning mostly through think-aloud and short experiments. Designers iterated far more on a creative problem (about 16 loops per session) than a routine one (about 4.5) [Chuslip & Jin, 2004](576), and constructive perception and visual reasoning each related to creative design performance, though not to each other [Kim et al., 2005](154). More causal information use went with more novel but lower-quality ideas [Abid et al., 2018](947).

6600|8255.text: Mental models appear in ideation studies as the knowledge designers bring to idea generation, tested mainly by adding physical models or functional representations. Building and testing physical models raised the fraction of functional ideas, which the authors read as supplementing mental models [Viswanathan & Linsey, 2010](649), while novelty fell in a costly building condition [Viswanathan & Linsey, 2011](608). Function decomposition helped students more than professionals' grades [Booth et al., 2015](977).

6600|8257.text: Studies combine ideation with analogy by giving designers biological descriptions, patents or near and far words, then comparing novelty, quality or fluency. Distance results differ: more distant patents led to more novel concepts [Venkataraman et al., 2017](934), while far analogies produced less novel best concepts than near ones [Fu et al., 2012](755). Telling students to consider how nature would solve the problem gave no significant gain [Glier et al., 2012](672).

6600|8259.text: Cognitive load shows up in concept generation studies through workload surveys, brain recordings and effort ratings. Load differed across design stages, and during ideation mental demand tracked idea uniqueness and usefulness ([Calpin & Menold, 2022](893)). Facilitated groups reported lower task load while producing more ideas than unfacilitated groups ([Murphy et al., 2023](50)); students using ChatGPT showed lower prefrontal effort ([Aruon et al., 2025](1460)), and warm-ups reduced stress without changing idea counts ([Hu et al., 2015](945)).

6600|8261.text: Concept-generation studies touch executive function only loosely, through process manipulations or brain measures. Ideation experiments found that suspending judgment raised idea quality but cut quantity ([Shah et al., 2006](358)). In a civil engineering course, students who used ChatGPT while thinking aloud identified more constraints and showed lower prefrontal effort on fNIRS ([Aruon et al., 2025](1460)). A protocol study linked creativity modes to activity patterns ([Kim et al., 2006](359)).

6600|8276.text: Team concept generation studies with students measured psychological safety through surveys alongside ideas or speaking turns. Psychological safety did not change how many ideas teams produced but predicted idea goodness ([Cole et al., 2020](1190)); more speaking turns predicted higher individual but not team safety ([O’Connell et al., 2022](861)). Trained facilitation raised idea quantity and psychological safety ([Murphy et al., 2023](50)).

6600|8277.text: Concept-generation studies treat problem-solving as the search process behind ideation, measured through protocol coding, brain sensing, or outcome scores. Compared with brainstorming, morphological analysis or TRIZ shifted students' attention from structure toward expected behavior ([Gero et al., 2012](728)) and produced repeated prefrontal activation ([Shealy et al., 2018](1047)). In morphological charts, students focused on the first columns regardless of order ([Chawla & Summers, 2018](955)).

6600|8280.text: Schema activation shows up in ideation studies through examples, information and prompts that bring up prior knowledge. Designers started with the most common solution categories and moved to novel ones, and example timing mattered more than commonness [Perttula & Liikkanen, 2006](361). Drawing people into concept sketches led to deeper reflections on users and fewer claims a design is for everyone [Makhlouf et al., 2023](43), and constructive perception related to creative performance [Kim et al., 2005](154).

6600|8281.text: Self-efficacy shows up in these concept-generation studies mostly as a side measure, usually drawing or design self-efficacy. In one, telling students their sketching would be evaluated had a negligible effect on idea generation ([Weaver et al., 2022](841)). Others measure related states: resilience and perceived scarcity predicted perceived design performance only for time scarcity ([Sibley et al., 2023](71)), and sketch warm-ups reduced stress without changing idea counts ([Hu et al., 2015](945)).

6600|8298.text: Incubation is tested with idea-generation tasks that include a break between sessions. Lab and design experiments both found it raised idea effectiveness ([Shah et al., 2003](298)), and incubation helped consistently across six ideation components ([Shah et al., 2006](358)). Distantly related information affected solutions only when given during a break ([Tseng et al., 2008](458)). Among industry professionals, few self-rated factors predicted outcomes ([Moreno et al., 2015](957)).

6600|8309.text: Working memory is approached through sketching chunks and brain activity during ideation. Most objects in a sketch were drawn in a single pen-stroke cluster, consistent with chunking ([Sen et al., 2017](1046)). Brainstorming produced an early left prefrontal response that was not sustained, unlike morphological analysis and TRIZ ([Shealy et al., 2018](1047)), while ideation sheets with more cells and fresh analogy images raised idea counts ([Batura & Camburn, 2025](1414)).

6600|8332.text: Studies gave students or practitioners a prior stimulus, such as a collage, example, word or analogy description, before or during idea generation, mostly in controlled experiments. Collage or questionnaire primes increased sustainability-related features and ideas ([She & MacDonald, 2012](690); [Liao & MacDonald, 2018](1111)), while similar information helped early and distant information helped only mid-task ([Tseng et al., 2008](458)). Not every study showed benefits; eliciting requirements first gave no advantage ([Joshi & Summers, 2014](1141)).

6600|8461.text: These studies connect concept generation with visual and spatial aspects of designing, such as sketching, drawn versus written representations, and judging the scale of turbine-blade reuse ideas. Graphical starting ideas gave more novel, higher-quality ideas than text ([McKoy et al., 2001](205)), and novices' sketching constrained idea development ([Radcliffe & Lee, 1994](1340)). One EEG study had a single participant.

6600|8523.text: Attention is mostly inferred indirectly in these ideation studies, through brain or skin recordings, mental-effort ratings or self-reported concentration. EEG showed more visual-thinking effort while generating than evaluating solutions ([Nguyen & Zeng, 2010](639)), and warm-up sketching lowered stress without changing idea counts ([Hu et al., 2015](945)). Self-rated concentration was one of many factors that mostly failed to predict ideation outcomes ([Moreno et al., 2015](957)).

6601|7836.text: Truss design is used both with student teams and with simulated agents, mainly to see how teams search and what drives performance. High-performing student teams chose simpler designs and explored small regions thoroughly ([McComb et al., 2014](1148)), and team performance depended mainly on the most proficient member ([Brownell et al., 2020](1186)). Simulated annealing teams tracked the human results closely ([McComb et al., 2015](1025)), and integrated optimization tools gave cheaper designs faster ([Burnell et al., 2017](1022)).

6601|7959.text: Robot and drone tasks pair optimization-style problems with agents or teams. A trust model raised success rate in a simulated box-pushing group, especially with many incompetent agents ([Ji & Jin, 2018](999)), nominal teams out-earned interacting ones in a drone fleet task ([Gyory et al., 2022](851)), and robotics participants at every expertise level fixated on an initial concept ([Wilson et al., 2023](81)).

6601|8049.text: Studies of optimization tools on parametric or mechanical problems are few and varied. A spreadsheet for preliminary parametric design was reported as intuitive and more supportive than a conventional one ([Ramaswamy & Ulrich, 1993](1497)). Giving designers learning goals raised learning scores, while performance goals produced better designs ([Chaudhari et al., 2021](908)). An algorithm for interactive search reached near-target designs in few comparisons ([Campbell et al., 2009](510)).

6601|8224.text: Design optimization of industrial equipment is mostly computational. A steam turbine design system raised efficiency by 1.3 percentage points and cut design time by an order of magnitude against an industrial case ([Jarrett et al., 2002](218)); a team-based agent algorithm improved solution quality by 65 percent ([Olson & Cagan, 2003](283)). Embedding operators' knowledge in a Bayesian optimizer cut setup iterations versus operators and standard optimization ([Dong et al., 2025](1449)).

6601|8230.text: The three papers show people using rules of thumb in optimization-like search and decision tasks. First search choices were not uniform: participants often bisected the range, anchored on prior data and favored whole numbers [Shergadwala & Panchal, 2020](1194), and students formed shared heuristics such as starting from the scrap part with most mounting points [Bjorni & Dinar, 2022](827). Requirement-style goals led to longer persistence and better scores than maximize framing [Malak et al., 2022](863).

6601|8233.text: Optimization studies connect to metacognition through reflection, understanding and learning during exploration. With an AI assistant, incubation improved satellite design performance more than reflection ([Song et al., 2023](74)). Robust optimization let students explore aircraft designs more efficiently with little difference in model understanding ([Pillai et al., 2020](1180)). Another study clustered logged behavior ([Rahman et al., 2021](901)).

6601|8238.text: Studies use truss, function-search or robot-design tasks, sometimes with simulated agents, and look for anchoring in search. First choices were not uniform: people bisected the range, anchored on prior data and favored whole numbers ([Shergadwala & Panchal, 2020](1194)), and robotics participants at all levels tended to fixate on their initial concept ([Wilson et al., 2023](81)). Strong truss teams explored small regions thoroughly ([McComb et al., 2014](1148)).

6601|8246.text: Cognitive style appears in studies of algorithmic and parameter-based design, with varied results. In agent simulations, style did not matter for a beam but more innovative teams did better on a race car ([Lapp et al., 2019](1024)). Clustering of CAD action logs found behavior groups that sometimes reached similar design quality ([Rahman et al., 2021](901)). Pair parameter studies linked short, steady actions to faster completion ([Avşar & Grogan, 2023](21)).

6601|8255.text: One of the three papers has no study details. Robust optimization let participants explore an aircraft design space more efficiently with little difference in model understanding ([Pillai et al., 2020](1180)), and a lab test of an automated turbine design system reported higher efficiency and shorter design time than an industrial case ([Jarrett et al., 2002](218)). A student exploration study is listed by title only.

6601|8259.text: Cognitive load appears only lightly alongside optimization-type tasks, so the evidence is limited. In a drone-fleet design task, nominal teams earned more than interacting ones but their managers reported heavier cognitive and workload burden ([Gyory et al., 2022](851)). Truss-design teams were compared on design complexity and exploration, not load ([McComb et al., 2014](1148)), and a trust-model simulation had no human participants ([Ji & Jin, 2018](999)).

6601|8267.text: These studies measure what designers learn while exploring design spaces with tools. A learning goal raised learning scores while a performance goal gave better designs ([Chaudhari et al., 2021](908)), incubation improved performance more than reflection when working with an AI assistant ([Song et al., 2023](74)), and different learning measures captured different knowledge among satellite design experts ([Bang & Selva, 2020](1181)).

6601|8277.text: People work on parameter or truss design tasks in software while an optimizer, algorithm or AI assistant is present or used as a benchmark. The best human performers behaved like a well-tuned simulated annealing algorithm and the worst nearly randomly ([Yu et al., 2015](1037)); an imposed search strategy helped ([Egan et al., 2014](1139)); more integrated optimization tools gave better designs faster ([Burnell et al., 2017](1022)).

6601|8302.text: Optimization tasks are combined with team influence in studies of how group interaction affects results. Teams that did not interact and chose their best member's solution did best on a cooling system problem ([McComb et al., 2017](986)), and team performance depended mainly on the strongest member, whose simpler designs teammates adopted ([Brownell et al., 2020](1186)). In simulation, cognitive style mattered for a race car but not a beam ([Lapp et al., 2019](1024)).

6602|8255.text: Participants draw or describe how a product is organized, and researchers read these drawings as evidence of their mental models, either from users or from students before and after teaching. Functional modeling instruction improved graduate students' drawings of household products, though the hair dryer likely hit a ceiling ([Murphy et al., 2019](1004)). A teardown did not change drawing scores, improved component identification and worsened functional reasoning ([Furiato & Murphy, 2024](20)).

6603|8252.text: Interviews, workshops and video are used to build or measure designers' empathy. Students who wore a mock prosthetic limb identified 95% of both lead-user and typical-user needs ([Vaughan et al., 2014](1163)); users and designers mimicked each other's facial expressions, which did not predict designers' understanding ([Salmi et al., 2022](847)); and preference accuracy showed no significant link to user satisfaction ([Johnson et al., 2023](28)).

6603|8523.text: The link to attention is indirect: the studies use observation or interviews around how designers find or notice information: slow online foraging for biological inspiration [Vattam & Goel, 2011](619), a calculated score for interview quality that did not track expert ratings [Grover et al., 2023](22), and an AI posture tool that improved the detail and efficiency of needs identified from video [Chong et al., 2025](1456).

6604|8018.text: Survey respondents evaluate consumer products, from sketches to printers, by rating, recall and difficulty judgments. Viewers recalled tangible aspects such as material and shape and preferred more informative sketches ([Sagan & Yang, 2012](743)). Customers' reported emotions matched napkin-dispenser message type ([Saadi & Yang, 2020](1183)), and users rated bed leveling as the most challenging printer problem ([Grey et al., 2022](885)).

6604|8233.text: Questionnaires in these studies capture self-reports tied to reflection and learning, though the four papers are quite different. Older adults' self-rated standing difficulty did not track therapist ratings or measured mobility [Stansfield et al., 2023](76), and students reported cost, time and perceived value of each prototype, with no significant link between cost and value [Nelson & Menold, 2020](1205). Interacting teams did worse than non-interacting teams on one problem [McComb et al., 2017](986).

6604|8238.text: Surveys address fixation mainly through expert opinion and practice. Experts at a conference were split on whether analogies cause fixation ([Krager et al., 2011](701)). Professional designers searching for examples mostly sought familiar or similar ones, which may limit benefit from diverse ones ([Miller & Bailey, 2014](1150)), and a survey of practitioners found informal concept selection ([Toh et al., 2015](1045)).

6604|8239.text: Surveys connect with divergent thinking in a few ways. Students took creativity tests and then listed bicycle accessory ideas; only the Alternative Uses Test predicted expert-rated creative ideas, with interest strengthening and familiarity weakening the link ([Kwon et al., 2017](914)). A music-playlist study used a short survey after ideation, and participants reported the video game playlist as most creative ([Wojciechowski et al., 2025](1419)). A conference survey asked experts about fixation ([Krager et al., 2011](701)).

6604|8246.text: Surveys or questionnaires gave measures of cognitive style, creativity mode or personality, which researchers related to ideation or team performance in workshops, courses and professional samples. Personality types differed in results across ideation methods ([Choo et al., 2014](1134)), and best-performing student teams had high variability in neuroticism and extraversion ([Lugo et al., 2017](990)). Studies are small and exploratory: regressions on thinking style produced hypotheses rather than conclusions ([Patel & Summers, 2021](874)).

6604|8250.text: Questionnaires capture emotions and experience ratings in studies of design courses, assistants and products. Students' retrospective ratings were lower for early research phases than later ones ([Moore et al., 2023](49)), and a bioinspired design course raised confidence and lowered anxiety ([Durand et al., 2015](917)). Napkin-dispenser messages matched different emotions such as encouragement or guilt ([Saadi & Yang, 2020](1183)); empathetic chatbot behavior raised trust ([Renji & Liao, 2025](1454)).

6604|8256.text: Trust is collected through post-task questionnaires, mostly about AI or autonomous tools, but also about teams and facilitators. In AI assistant studies, better system performance and empathetic behavior raised trust ([Renji & Liao, 2025](1454)), while affective priming did not change overall trust in a voice assistant ([Liao & MacDonald, 2019](1075)). In a workshop, facilitator behaviors correlated positively with team trust and psychological safety ([Witherell et al., 2024](83)).

6604|8257.text: Surveys and questionnaires accompany analogy work as follow-ups or as stand-alone opinion polls. After sketching with analogy sets, participants rated distant-domain analogies as less useful, though those domains produced at least as many ideas and emergent features ([Lopez et al., 2011](613)). Experts were split on whether analogies cause fixation ([Krager et al., 2011](701)). Other surveys cover problem familiarity and analogies ([Durand et al., 2015](949)) or viewers' recall of sketches ([Sagan & Yang, 2012](743)).

6604|8258.text: Online surveys measured how risky people judged designs or their own engineering decisions. Perceived vehicle safety varied with personal traits and experience, with shape the most influential feature ([Cai et al., 2019](1071)). Engineering students completed a new risk attitude test that was reliable overall, though factor analysis suggested other domains fit better ([Bossuyt et al., 2011](678)), and questionnaire risk attitudes barely improved prediction of strategic choices ([Avşar et al., 2022](865)).

6604|8259.text: Workload and effort are collected through ratings such as NASA-TLX, RSME or burden questionnaires after design or lab tasks. Results vary: an AI assistant did not significantly change mental workload ([Maier et al., 2019](992)), trained facilitation lowered perceived task load ([Murphy et al., 2023](50)), managers in nominal teams carried heavier burden ([Gyory et al., 2022](851)), and perceived burden in lab tasks depended strongly on reagent properties ([Jung & Bruns, 2024](29)).

6604|8265.text: Surveys on team composition and interaction are the common link, with cohesion not always the headline measure. Constraining teams by personality preference raised the share of prize-winning student teams from 29 to 60 percent ([Wilde, 1997](1694)), and surveys fed a simulation of virtual versus face-to-face teams ([Singh et al., 2021](846)). Email networks identified teams with high conflict ([Sitarama & Agogino, 2022](843)).

6604|8267.text: Course studies pair questionnaires with learning-related measures such as pre- and post-tests or perceived learning value. Test scores rose on all four questions after students used multimedia motor software ([Reamon & Sheppard, 1999](1626)), no significant link was found between prototype cost and perceived value or outcome, with top teams valuing final prototypes less for learning ([Nelson & Menold, 2020](1205)), and a logging device captured requirements and goals between iterations ([Nelson et al., 2019](1083)).

6604|8274.text: These surveys paired lottery-based risk measures with follow-up tasks or background questions, using students and one group of professionals. Risk-averse students generated and chose less creative ideas ([Toh & Miller, 2014](1142)), while risk attitude did not predict prototype choice ([Starkey et al., 2018](1097)). Among professionals, education and experience related to creative risk-taking ([Zheng & Miller, 2017](1018)), and choice-based risk estimates predicted strategic decisions better than the questionnaire ([Avşar et al., 2022](865)).

6604|8275.text: Surveys on risk propensity are mostly questionnaires or lottery items given to engineering students and industry staff, and they show that measuring risk attitude is not simple. A new engineering-specific test was reliable overall, but factor analysis suggested other domains fit engineers better [Bossuyt et al., 2011](678). Questionnaire-based attitudes barely improved prediction of strategic design choices, while attitudes inferred from choices did far better [Avşar et al., 2022](865).

6604|8276.text: Psychological safety is usually measured with short seven-item or five-item surveys given repeatedly to student design teams. Scores stabilized only after idea generation began and varied widely across teams ([Miller et al., 2019](1012)); they did not change over two capstone semesters, with or without industry mentors ([Arpini-Lorenzoni et al., 2024](3)). Gender composition did not change safety, but women felt safer with women ([Cole et al., 2022](857)); facilitation raised it ([Murphy et al., 2023](50)).

6604|8281.text: Self-efficacy is collected by questionnaire, mostly in design courses or workshops, often next to idea or team outcomes. A bioinspired design course raised students' design confidence and lowered anxiety ([Durand et al., 2015](917)), self-rated psychological factors predicted few ideation outcomes among professionals ([Moreno et al., 2015](957)), and design self-efficacy did not correlate with how students clustered product elements ([Patel et al., 2023](59)). Virtual teams reported higher self-efficacy than face-to-face ones ([Singh et al., 2021](846)).
